Theory 1.1 Conditional Probability and the Reduced Sample Space The conditional probability of an event , given that an event has already occurred, denoted by , is defined as: If , the conditional probability is undefined; conditioning on an impossible event provides no reference framework within classical probability theory. Acquiring partial information modifies the effective universe of outcomes. In the absence of extra information, probabilities are measured relative to the global sample space , where . Once it is known that event has occurred, every outcome residing in the complement becomes impossible. The sample space collapses from to a reduced sample space consisting exclusively of the outcomes in . Within this contracted subspace, an event can occur if and only if the observed outcome belongs to the intersection . Because the total probability assigned to the new universe must equal , dividing by acts as a normalizing constant that rescales the relative probability mass of all surviving outcomes in : 1.1.1 Directional Asymmetry: Flight Punctuality Conditional probability is intrinsically directional: conditioning on given is fundamentally different from conditioning on given . In general: Consider an airline tracking flight records: Let be the event that a flight departs on time: . Let be the event that a flight arrives on time: . Let be the event that a flight departs and arrives on time: . Evaluating the two distinct conditioning directions: Probability that a flight arrives on time, given that it departed on time: Probability that a flight departed on time, given that it arrived on time: Although both conditional quantities rely on the same joint intersection probability , their normalizing baselines differ ( versus ), yielding . 1.1.2 Contraction of Sample Space: The Loaded Die The mechanics of sample space reduction become transparent when assigning non-uniform probabilities across discrete elementary outcomes. Consider a biased six-sided die where even outcomes are constructed to be twice as likely as odd outcomes. The universal sample space is . Let denote the probability weight of each odd outcome , and let denote the weight of each even outcome . Except in the special case where , these values are strictly unequal. Confusing the Joint Intersection with Conditional Probability: Mistaking for . The joint probability measures the likelihood that both and occur simultaneously relative to the whole universe . The conditional probability measures the likelihood of occurring within the restricted sub-universe . Because , it always holds that . Conditioning on Null-Probability Events: Attempting to apply when . Division by zero is undefined, reflecting the fact that conditioning on an impossible event provides no empirical or mathematical subspace to renormalize. 1.2 Independence of Two Events Two events and are statistically independent (or simply independent) if and only if: assuming that the respective conditional probabilities exist (i.e., and ). If neither equality holds, the events are dependent. Using the general multiplication relation , substituting yields the equivalent and universal product formulation of independence: This product definition holds unconditionally, even if or . Statistical independence formalizes the concept of informational neutrality: learning that event has occurred provides zero predictive information about whether event will occur, leaving the posterior probability of identical to its prior baseline . 1.2.1 Worked Illustration: Independence Within a Single Trial A common misconception is that independent events must stem from separate, unrelated experiments (such as two distinct coin tosses). Events originating from a single trial can be completely independent. Consider rolling a single fair six-sided die. The sample space is , where each simple outcome has probability . Define: Event : Rolling an even number Event : Rolling a multiple of The prior probabilities are: The intersection represents rolling a number that is both even and a multiple of : Testing via the product rule: Equivalently, conditioning on : Because , knowing that the roll resulted in a multiple of ( ) does not alter the probability that the result is even ( ). Thus, and are statistically independent despite being properties of the exact same physical die roll. 1.2.2 Common Pitfalls: Independence vs. Mutual Exclusivity The most frequent error is conflating independence with mutual exclusivity (disjointness): Mutual Exclusivity is an operational property of sets: , meaning the two events cannot occur simultaneously. Consequently: Independence is an informational balance of probability measures: If two events and have positive probabilities ( and ), they cannot be both mutually exclusive and independent: If they are mutually exclusive, then . For them to also be independent, it would require , yielding , a contradiction. If two non-trivial events are mutually exclusive, they are maximally dependent: knowing that occurred guarantees that did not occur ( ). 1.3 The Multiplication Rule for Two Events The multiplication rule (or product rule) provides a formula for the probability of the joint occurrence (intersection) of two events. Formally, if in an experiment the events and can both occur, then: Because set intersection is symmetric ( ), the rule can be evaluated conditioning on either event: When two events are independent, the occurrence of one does not affect the probability of the other, meaning and . Under independence, the general multiplication rule specializes to: Two events and are independent if and only if this factorization holds. The multiplication rule allows the calculation of joint probabilities from an initial probability and an updated conditional probability. It translates physical step-by-step mechanisms—such as stages in a multi-step inspection, time-ordered physical events, or parallel systems—into compound probabilistic models. 1.3.1 Dependent Sequential Sampling: The Defective Fuses Consider sampling without replacement, where an action at step one alters the composition of the sample space for step two. A box contains fuses, of which are defective and are operational. Two fuses are selected at random and removed in succession without replacement. Let: be the event that the first fuse is defective. be the event that the second fuse is defective. The joint event corresponds to drawing defective fuses on both selections: On the first draw, the probability of obtaining a defective fuse from the original pool is: Given that event occurred, the box now contains fuses, of which are defective. The conditional probability is: Applying the general multiplication rule: Because , the successive selections are dependent. 1.3.2 Independent Systems: Emergency Vehicle Readiness In contrast to sequential sampling, parallel systems often involve events that do not exert physical influence on one another. A municipal emergency center maintains one fire engine and one ambulance. Historical readiness logs show: The probability that the fire engine is available when called is . The probability that the ambulance is available when called is . Assuming the dispatch operations of the two vehicles are independent, the probability that both vehicles are simultaneously ready to respond to a structural fire with casualties is: 1.3.3 Common Pitfalls Assuming Independence by Default: Calculating as when sampling without replacement or when prior stages alter the underlying conditions. The simplified formula applies only when events are proven or established to be independent. Direction of Conditioning Confusion: Believing that . The factor conditioning on must multiply the marginal probability of , giving , whereas conditioning on requires . Equating Intersection with Conditional Likelihood: Conflating with . measures the probability of both events occurring within the original sample space , whereas assesses the probability of relative to the contracted subspace . 1.4 General Chain Rule and Mutual Independence of Multiple Events The general chain rule (also known as the multiplication rule for events) generalizes conditional probability to the intersection of an arbitrary collection of events . For any sequence of events where the conditional probabilities are defined ( ), the joint probability satisfies: The chain rule decomposes the joint occurrence of many interdependent stages into a product of one-step conditional updates. Each successive event is evaluated against the accumulated history of all prior outcomes, making it the mathematical foundation for analyzing multi-stage processes and sequential sampling without replacement. 1.4.1 Sequential Card Selection Without Replacement Consider an ordinary 52-card deck from which three cards are dealt in succession without replacement. Define the sequence of events: : The first card is a red ace. : The second card is a 10 or a jack. : The third card is strictly between 3 and 7 (i.e., a 4, 5, or 6). To find the probability that all three events occur in sequence, apply the chain rule step-by-step: First draw ( ): A standard deck contains 2 red aces (Ace of Hearts, Ace of Diamonds) out of 52 cards: Second draw conditioned on ( ): Exactly 51 cards remain. The red ace drawn did not affect the pool of 10s and jacks, which consists of 4 tens and 4 jacks (8 cards total): Third draw conditioned on ( ): Exactly 50 cards remain. Ranks strictly between 3 and 7 are 4, 5, and 6. Across 4 suits, there are such cards. Neither prior draw removed any 4, 5, or 6: Multiplying these sequential probabilities via the chain rule yields: 1.4.2 Mutual Independence of Multiple Events A finite collection of events is mutually independent (or simply independent) if and only if for every subset of size , the probability of their intersection equals the product of their individual probabilities: For an arbitrary collection of events, mutual independence requires that all distinct subset product conditions hold simultaneously. For three events , mutual independence requires satisfying four distinct equations: When mutual independence holds across , conditioning on any subset of other events provides zero new information ( ), and the general chain rule collapses directly to the unfiltered product: 1.4.3 Insufficiency of Whole-Set Factorization A common misconception is that mutual independence across events can be established solely by verifying the single top-level relation . This condition alone is strictly insufficient. Consider three events , , and defined such that: and are identical, non-trivial events: with . is the impossible event, meaning . Evaluating the total joint intersection: Evaluating the product of all three individual probabilities: The product factorization holds identically. However, events and are not independent: Because , knowing occurred completely determines that occurred ( ). Hence, whole-set factorization can hold accidentally due to a degenerate component without guaranteeing genuine independence among the constituent pairs. 1.4.4 Common Pitfalls Pairwise Independence vs. Mutual Independence: Pairwise independence ( for all ) does not imply mutual independence, nor does whole-set factorization imply pairwise independence. Full mutual independence strictly requires verifying every subset equation of every order . Static Denominators in Sequential Conditioning: Forgetting to update both the numerator and the denominator at each successive stage of the chain rule. In sampling without replacement, the sample space contracts ( ), and prior selections permanently deplete specific subsets of available items. 1.5 The Law of Total Probability A collection of events is called a partition of the sample space if the events satisfy three conditions: 1. Pairwise mutually exclusive: for all . 2. Exhaustive: . 3. Non-zero probabilities: for each . The Law of Total Probability expresses the marginal probability of any event as a weighted sum of the conditional probabilities of across the partition classes : 1.5.1 Motivation and Theoretical Derivation Directly computing is often intractable when occurs as the culmination of an experiment with multiple pathways, intermediate stages, or hidden regimes. Conditioning on a well-chosen partition breaks the complex event into simpler, localized scenarios where the conditional probabilities are straightforward to determine. Theorem (Law of Total Probability): Let be a partition of with for each . For any event : Proof: Because is exhaustive ( ), we express via intersection with the entire sample space: By the distributive law of set theory, the intersection distributes across the union: Since the events are pairwise disjoint ( for ), their intersections with are also pairwise disjoint: By the finite additivity axiom of probability measures, the probability of a union of pairwise disjoint events is the sum of their individual probabilities: Applying the multiplication rule to each term in the summation yields: 1.5.2 Worked Mini-Illustration: Two-Stage Transfer Experiment A classic multi-stage application involves transferring an item between containers without replacement before a terminal draw: Bag 1 contains white balls and black balls ( balls total). Bag 2 contains white balls and black balls ( balls total). One ball is drawn at random from Bag 1 and placed unseen into Bag 2. A ball is then drawn from Bag 2. We wish to find the probability that the ball drawn from Bag 2 is black ( ). Define the partition: The unseen ball transferred from Bag 1 must be either black ( ) or white ( ). These two events form a valid partition of the first stage because and . Evaluate the conditional probabilities: If a black ball was transferred ( ), Bag 2 now holds white and black balls ( balls total): If a white ball was transferred ( ), Bag 2 now holds white and black balls ( balls total): Apply the Law of Total Probability: Decomposing the outcome by the unseen intermediate transfer step resolves an otherwise intractable sequential dependency. 1.5.3 Common Pitfalls Incomplete or Overlapping Partitions: Using events that fail to cover the entire space (omitting cases) or events that are not mutually exclusive ( ). If is not a strict partition, due to either missing probability mass or double-counted intersections. Static Denominator Error in Dynamic Transfers: Forgetting to update the total count or color composition of the second stage when conditioning. In the transfer example above, the total number of balls in Bag 2 increases from to ; treating the second-stage sample size as unchanged produces invalid conditionals. Confusing with : The Law of Total Probability requires the forward conditional probabilities weighted by prior stage probabilities . Inverting them to confuses cause and effect (which requires Bayes’ rule). 1.6 Bayes’ Rule and Posterior Inference Bayes’ Rule (or Bayes’ Theorem) provides a formal mathematical procedure for inverting conditional probabilities. It determines the probability that a specific underlying cause or partition state occurred given that a particular piece of evidence has been observed. Likelihood ( ): The probability of observing evidence assuming hypothesis is true. Marginal Likelihood / Total Evidence ( ): The overall probability of observing evidence across all possible mutual states; it acts as a normalizing constant ensuring that . Posterior Probability ( ): The updated belief that state holds after accounting for the observed evidence . 1.6.3 Worked Illustration: Manufacturing Source Attribution A factory operates three machines— —producing , , and of total output, respectively. The probabilities that an item manufactured by these machines is defective ( ) are known from historical monitoring: A finished item is drawn at random and found to be defective ( ). We evaluate the posterior probability that it originated from machine : Calculate the joint probabilities (the partition slices): Sum to obtain the marginal probability of defect : Compute the posterior probability : The observation of a defect updates the likelihood that machine was responsible from a prior of ( ) to a posterior of ( ). 1.6.4 Common Pitfalls The Base Rate Fallacy: Ignoring the prior and equating with . Even if a likelihood is large, a minuscule prior can keep the posterior very low. Denominator Incompleteness: Failing to sum over all components of the partition in the denominator. The denominator must include every mutually exclusive path capable of generating event . 1.7 Random Variables and Sample Space Classification A random variable is a real-valued function that maps every outcome in a sample space to a real number: For each element , the function assigns a deterministic value . The term “variable” is historically entrenched, but mathematically is neither a variable nor a single static number; it is a deterministic rule that translates physical or qualitative experimental outcomes into numerical measurements. Capital letters such as denote the random variable itself (the mapping function), whereas lowercase letters such as denote specific, realized numerical values that the random variable can assume. 1.7.1 The Pre-Image and Event Formulation Random variables bridge sample spaces and quantitative probability theory. Instead of managing complex collections of raw descriptions (such as sequences of heads, tails, parts, or failure modes), random variables assign numbers to these descriptions so that algebraic, calculus, and statistical operations can be applied. Because maps outcomes to real numbers, any mathematical statement regarding corresponds to an event (a subset of ) via the pre-image of the function: Similarly, inequality conditions define inverse image events: The probability is formally defined as the probability of the underlying subset: Consider an experiment where three electronic components are inspected in succession. Let denote a defective component and denote a nondefective component. The sample space contains elementary outcomes: Let denote the random variable representing the total number of defective components found. Then can take any integer value in . The numerical statement corresponds to the specific event subset: Assigning a probability to the numerical realization means evaluating the aggregate probability of the event . 1.7.2 Canonical Mappings: Urn Extractions and Indicator Variables The mapping from qualitative outcomes to numerical values partitions the sample space into mutually exclusive subsets based on the realized value. Urn Extraction Without Replacement: An urn contains red balls and black balls. Two balls are drawn in succession without replacement. The sample space consists of ordered pairs indicating the color of the first and second ball: Let denote the random variable representing the number of red balls drawn. The mapping evaluates each outcome: Outcome Realized Value Underlying Event Pre-Image Each realized value collapses multiple structural paths into an equivalent count. Indicator (Bernoulli) Variables: When an experiment classifies items into binary categories (e.g., success/failure, active/inactive, defective/nondefective), the classification is formalized via an indicator variable (or Bernoulli random variable). Let a component arriving from a manufacturing line be evaluated: If is the event that the component is defective, then is the indicator function : This transforms set-membership questions into arithmetic terms, since and . 1.7.3 Discrete versus Continuous Sample Spaces Sample spaces are classified based on the cardinality of their constituent elements, which directly determines the nature of the random variables defined upon them. Discrete Sample Space: A sample space is discrete if it consists of a finite number of outcomes or a countably infinite sequence of outcomes (elements that can be put into a one-to-one correspondence with the whole numbers ). Finite example: Testing electronic components yields outcomes. Countably infinite example: Counting the number of tosses of a coin required until the first head appears produces , which is countably infinite. Continuous Sample Space: A sample space is continuous if it contains an uncountably infinite number of possibilities, corresponding to all points within a continuum, line segment, or real interval. Uncountable example: Measuring the exact time (in seconds) until an unstable radioactive particle decays yields: Because time can assume any non-negative real value along the continuum, no list indexed by whole numbers can enumerate all possible outcomes. 1.7.4 Common Pitfalls Treating as an Algebraic Unknown: In algebra, represents an unknown number to be solved (e.g., ). In probability, a random variable is an explicit function mapping the sample space to . Writing does not mean is algebraically replaced by ; it denotes the inverse image event . Conflating the Realized Value with the Function : is the rule (e.g., “count the defective components”), whereas is a specific number in its range (e.g., ). Writing without defining obscures the underlying mapping. Confusing the Outcome Space with the Variable’s Range: The elements of can be non-numeric symbols, text, sequences, or physical objects (e.g., ), while the values taken by are strictly numbers in . A random variable does not create randomness; it merely assigns real numbers to the random outcomes generated by an experiment. 1.8 Probability Mass Functions (PMF) and Hypergeometric Modeling For a discrete random variable , the rule assigning probabilities to each realizable numerical value is formalized by its probability distribution. The set of ordered pairs is called the probability function, probability distribution, or probability mass function (PMF) of , denoted mathematically as: A function qualifies as a valid probability mass function if and only if it satisfies the following three axiomatic conditions for every possible real number : Non-negativity: Total probability normalization: Event evaluation: The summation in condition (2) extends over all distinct values within the support of (the set of values where ). The PMF compresses an arbitrary sample space into a functional model that maps numeric experimental outcomes directly to their corresponding probability masses. 1.8.1 Constructing a PMF: Three Coin Tosses Consider flipping a balanced coin three times independently. The underlying sample space consists of equally likely elementary outcomes: Let the discrete random variable denote the total number of heads observed ( ). The number of distinct subsets of size drawn from a collection of distinct items is given by the binomial coefficient: where . Combinations form the combinatorial foundation for modeling selections from finite groups without replacement. 1.8.3 The Hypergeometric Distribution When drawing a random sample without replacement from a finite population containing two distinct categories of items (often labeled “successes/defectives” versus “failures/non-defectives”), the trial outcomes are dependent. The resulting probability mass function is the hypergeometric distribution. Let: be the total population size, be the number of defective (or marked) items in the population, be the number of non-defective items in the population, be the sample size drawn without replacement ( ), be the random variable counting the number of defective items in the sample. The probability of obtaining exactly defective items in the sample is: The support of is constrained by both the sample size and the population composition: The denominator counts the total number of equally likely ways to select items from . In the numerator, counts the ways to choose defectives from the available, and counts the ways to choose the remaining non-defectives from the non-defectives. 1.8.4 Worked Example: Laptop Purchase Selection A retail shipment consists of identical laptop computers, of which are defective and are non-defective. A school randomly purchases laptops without replacement. Let denote the number of defective laptops received. The possible values for are . The total number of unconstrained pairs is: We evaluate the PMF for each admissible value: Zero defective laptops ( ): One defective laptop ( ): Two defective laptops ( ): The complete probability distribution table is: Validating the sum condition: 1.8.5 Common Pitfalls Assuming Independence (Binomial vs. Hypergeometric): Treating finite-population sampling without replacement as independent trials. If sampling occurred with replacement, the probability of a defective laptop would remain constant at (binomial model). Because sampling occurs without replacement, the pool depletes after each selection, altering subsequent probabilities and mandating the hypergeometric model. Invalid Support Bounds: Attempting to evaluate outside physical boundaries, such as setting (selecting more defectives than exist) or (requiring more non-defectives than are present in the lot). For those impossible values, combinations evaluate to zero ( when ). Confusing the PMF with the CDF: The PMF represents pointwise probability , whereas the cumulative distribution function (CDF) aggregates probability up to that threshold: . 1.9 Cumulative Distribution Functions (CDF) for Discrete Random Variables The cumulative distribution function (often abbreviated as CDF), denoted by , of a discrete random variable with probability mass function is defined for all real numbers as: While the probability mass function gives the probability that takes a single exact value, the cumulative distribution function accumulates the total probability mass at or below a given threshold . This representation is essential because practical engineering and risk scenarios frequently require evaluating threshold probabilities (such as the chance of experiencing at most failures or finding at most defective items) rather than isolated point probabilities. 1.9.1 Structural Properties of a Discrete CDF Because is discrete, its CDF possesses distinct analytical properties across the real line : Domain and Range: The domain is the entire real line, , not merely the support points of . The range is bounded within the closed interval , with asymptotic limits: Step-Function Profile: The function is a piecewise constant step function. It remains flat on each interval between consecutive support values where no new probability mass exists. Jump Discontinuities: At every support point where , the graph experiences an upward vertical jump. The magnitude of this jump corresponds precisely to the probability mass at that location: Right-Continuity: Discrete CDFs are right-continuous everywhere, written mathematically as for all . At each jump discontinuity , the function value includes the jump (the point is a solid dot, whereas the segment approaching from the left terminates in an open circle). 1.9.2 Worked Construction: The Laptop Inspection Distribution Consider the shipment of laptops containing defectives, from which a random sample of laptops is purchased without replacement. Solution Two main functions are: Resource management Provide fine abstractions from the bare metal Question 2 In Section 1.4, nine different types of operating systems are described. Give a list of applications for each of these systems (one per operating systems type). Solution There are a lot of possible answers. Here are some. Mainframe operating system: Sales reporting for a chain of stores. Server operating system: Speech-to-text conversion service for intelligent assistant Alice. Multiprocessor operating system: Video editing and rendering. Personal computer operating system: Word processing application. Handheld computer operating system: PDA (Personal Digital Assistant) that can be held in your hand during operation. Embedded operating system: Programming a DVD recorder for recording TV. Sensor-node operating system: Glean information about enemy movements on battlefields. Real-time operating system: Air traffic control system. Smart-card operating system: Electronic payment. Question 3 (Tutorial 1) What is the difference between timesharing and multiprogramming systems? Solution Multiprogramming is the allocation of multiple programs on one computer simultaneously. Time-sharing is the sharing of computing resources among several users at the same time. All timesharing systems are multiprogramming systems but not all multiprogramming systems are timesharing systems. Question 4 To use cache memory, main memory is divided into cache lines, typically 32 or 64 bytes long. An entire cache line is cached at once. What is the advantage of caching an entire line instead of a single byte or word at a time? Solution Because of locality of reference: if one word is accessed, nearby words — especially the following ones — will very likely be accessed soon, so caching the whole line raises the hit rate. Also, one 32- or 64-byte block transfer is much faster than reading the same bytes word by word. Question 5 On early computers, every byte of data read or written was handled by the CPU (i.e., there was no DMA). What implications does this have for multiprogramming? Solution The prime reason for multiprogramming is to give the CPU something to do while waiting for I/O to complete. If there is no DMA, the CPU is fully occupied doing I/O, so there is nothing to be gained (at least in terms of CPU utilization) by multiprogramming. No matter how much I/O a program does, the CPU will be 100% busy. This of course assumes the major delay is the wait while data are copied. A CPU could do other work if the I/O were slow for other reasons (arriving on a serial line, for instance). Question 6 Instructions related to accessing I/O devices are typically privileged instructions, that is, they can be executed in kernel mode but not in user mode. Give a reason why these instructions are privileged. Solution Access to I/O devices (e.g., a printer) is typically restricted for different users. Some users may be allowed to print as many pages as they like, others nothing at all, others only a quota. The system administrator sets such per-user policies, and they can only be enforced if user programs cannot touch the device directly — hence the privilege. Question 7 The family-of-computers idea was introduced in the 1960s with the IBM System/360 mainframes. Is this idea now dead as a doornail or does it live on? Solution It is still alive. For example, Intel makes Core i3, i5, and i7 CPUs with a variety of different properties including speed and power consumption. All of these machines are architecturally compatible. They differ only in price and performance, which is the essence of the family idea. Question 8 (Tutorial 1) One reason GUIs were initially slow to be adopted was the cost of the hardware needed to support them. How much video RAM is needed to support a 25-line × 80-row character monochrome text screen? How much for a 1200 × 900-pixel 24-bit color bitmap? What was the cost of this RAM at 1980 prices ( 15,820. Question 9 There are several design goals in building an operating system, for example, resource utilization, timeliness, robustness, and so on. Give an example of two design goals that may contradict one another. Solution Consider fairness and real time. Fairness requires that each process be allocated its resources in a fair way, with no process getting more than its fair share. On the other hand, real time requires that resources be allocated based on the times when different processes must complete their execution. A realtime process may get a disproportionate share of the resources. Question 10 (Tutorial 1, Pre-Final 2020) What is the difference between kernel and user mode? Explain how having two distinct modes aids in designing an operating system. Solution In Kernel mode, the executing code has complete access to the underlying hardware. It can execute any CPU instruction and reference any memory address. Kernel mode is generally reserved for the lowest-level, most trusted functions of the operating system. Crashes in kernel mode are catastrophic; they will halt the entire PC. In User mode, the executing code cannot directly access hardware or reference memory. Code running in user mode must delegate to system APIs to access hardware or memory. Due to the protection afforded by this sort of isolation, crashes in user mode are always recoverable. Question 11 (Retake 2 2017) A 255-GB disk has 65,536 cylinders with 255 sectors per track and 512 bytes per sector. How many platters and heads does this disk have? Assuming an average cylinder seek time of 11 ms, average rotational delay of 7 ms and reading rate of 100 MB/s, calculate the average time it will take to read 400 KB from one sector. Solution One cylinder holds 255 × 512 bytes per head, so the head count is 255 × 2³⁰ / (65,536 × 255 × 512) = 32 heads, i.e. 16 platters (two heads each). A read takes seek + rotational latency + transfer: 11 ms + 7 ms + 400 KB / 100 MB/sec = 11 + 7 + 4 = 22 ms on average. Question 12 Which of the following instructions should be allowed only in kernel mode? Disable all interrupts. Read the time-of-day clock. Set the time-of-day clock. Change the memory map. Solution Choices (a), (c), and (d) should be restricted to kernel mode: disabling interrupts would let a user hang the whole machine; setting the clock would break accounting and file timestamps; changing the memory map would break every process’s protection. Reading the clock (b) is harmless and stays available. Question 13 (Tutorial 1) Consider a system that has two CPUs, each CPU having two threads (hyperthreading). Suppose three programs: P0, P1, and P2, are started with run times of 5, 10 and 20 ms, respectively. How long will it take to complete the execution of these programs? Assume that all three programs are 100% CPU bound, do not block during execution, and do not change CPUs once assigned. Solution This system consists of two physical CPUs where each CPU has 2 threads (logical processors). In total, there are 4 logical processors in the system. The time required to complete the execution of these 3 programs (P0, P1, and P2), depends on how the operating system schedules them: If P0 and P1 are scheduled on the same CPU (will take 10 msec if P0 and P1 are running simultaneously on different logical processors, OR will take 15 msec if both programs are sequentially running on the same logical processor), and P2 is scheduled on the other CPU (will take 20 msec). In result, it will take 20 msec to complete the execution of all programs. If P0 and P2 are scheduled on the same CPU (will take 20 msec if P0 and P2 are running simultaneously on different logical processors, OR will take 25 msec if both programs are sequentially running on the same logical processor), and P1 is scheduled on the other CPU (will take 10 msec). In result, it will take 25 msec to complete the execution of all programs. If P1 and P2 are scheduled on the same CPU (will take 20 msec if P1 and P2 are running simultaneously on different logical processors, OR will take 30 msec if both programs are sequentially running on the same logical processor), and P0 is scheduled on the other CPU (will take 5 msec). In result, it will take 30 msec to complete the execution of all programs. If all three are on the same CPU (will take 20 msec if P0 and P1 are running sequentially on the same logical processor, whereas P2 is running on the other logical processor, OR will take 25 msec if P0 and P2 are running sequentially on the same logical processor, whereas P1 is running on the other logical processor, OR will take 30 msec if P1 and P2 are running sequentially on the same logical processor, whereas P0 is running on the other logical processor, OR will take 35 msec if all three programs are sequentially running on the same logical processor). In result, it will take 35 msec to complete the execution of all programs. Question 14 A computer has a pipeline with four stages. Each stage takes the same time to do its work, namely, 1 ns. How many instructions per second can this machine execute? Solution Every nanosecond one instruction emerges from the pipeline. This means the machine is executing 1 billion instructions per second. It does not matter at all how many stages the pipeline has. A 10-stage pipeline with 1 ns per stage would also execute 1 billion instructions per second. All that matters is how often a finished instruction pops out the end of the pipeline. Question 15 (Tutorial 1) Consider a computer system that has cache memory, main memory (RAM) and disk, and an operating system that uses virtual memory. It takes 1 ns to access a word from the cache, 10 ns to access a word from the RAM, and 10 ms to access a word from the disk. If the cache hit rate is 95% and main memory hit rate (after a cache miss) is 99%, what is the average time to access a word? Solution Average access time = 0.95 × 1 nsec (word is in cache) + 0.05 × 0.99 × 10 nsec (in RAM, not in cache) + 0.05 × 0.01 × 10,000,000 nsec (on disk only) = 5001.445 nsec = 5.001445 µsec Question 16 (Retake 2 2017) When a user program makes a system call to read or write a disk file, it provides an indication of which file it wants, a pointer to the data buffer, and the count. Control is then transferred to the operating system, which calls the appropriate driver. Suppose that the driver starts the disk and terminates until an interrupt occurs. In the case of reading from the disk, obviously the caller will have to be blocked (because there are no data for it). What about the case of writing to the disk? Need the caller be blocked awaiting completion of the disk transfer? Solution Maybe. If the caller gets control back and immediately overwrites the data, when the write finally occurs, the wrong data will be written. However, if the driver first copies the data to a private buffer before returning, then the caller can be allowed to continue immediately. Another possibility is to allow the caller to continue and give it a signal when the buffer may be reused, but this is tricky and error prone. Question 17 What is a trap instruction? Explain its use in operating systems. Solution A trap is a synchronous interrupt caused by the running program itself: either a dedicated trap instruction (e.g. syscall on x86-64) executed deliberately to request an operating-system service, or a CPU-detected exception such as division by 0 or floating-point underflow. In all cases the trap switches the CPU from user mode to kernel mode and hands control to the operating system. Its main use is implementing system calls: the library procedure puts the number of the requested call in a register and traps; the kernel dispatches to the right handler and, when done, returns to the instruction following the call. Question 18 (Retake 1 2017) Why is the process table needed in a timesharing system? Is it also needed in personal computer systems running UNIX or Windows with a single user? Solution The process table is needed to store the state of a process that is currently suspended, either ready or blocked. Modern personal computer systems have dozens of processes running even when the user is doing nothing and no programs are open. They are checking for updates, loading email, and many other things. On a UNIX system, use the ps -a command to see them. On a Windows system, use the task manager. Question 19 (Retake 2.2 2016, Final 2017) Is there any reason why you might want to mount a file system on a nonempty directory? If so, what is it? Solution Mounting a file system makes any files already in the mount-point directory inaccessible, so mount points are normally empty. However, a system administrator might want to copy some of the most important files normally located in the mounted directory to the mount point so they could be found in their normal path in an emergency when the mounted device was being repaired. Question 20 (Retake 1 2016) For each of the following system calls, give a condition that causes it to fail: fork, exec, and unlink. Solution Fork can fail if there are no free slots left in the process table (and possibly if there is no memory or swap space left). Exec can fail if the file name given does not exist or is not a valid executable file. Unlink can fail if the file to be unlinked does not exist or the calling process does not have the authority to unlink it. Question 21 (Retake 2.1 2016) What type of multiplexing (time, space, or both) can be used for sharing the following resources: CPU, memory, disk, network card, printer, keyboard, and display? Solution Time multiplexing: CPU, network card, printer, keyboard. Space multiplexing: memory, disk. Both: display. Question 22 Can the call count = write(fd, buffer, nbytes); return any value in count other than nbytes? If so, why? Solution Yes. The call returns the number of bytes actually written. Normally that equals nbytes, but it may be smaller — for example, if the disk fills up in the middle of the write so only part of the data could be stored (the exact analog of read, which returns a short count at end-of-file). If the call cannot be carried out at all — e.g. fd is not a valid open descriptor or a disk error occurs — it returns −1 and the error number is put in errno, so programs must always check the result. Question 23 A file whose file descriptor is fd contains the following sequence of bytes: 3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6, 5, 3, 5. The following system calls are made: lseek(fd, 3, SEEK_SET); read(fd, &buffer, 4); where the lseek call makes a seek to byte 3 of the file. What does buffer contain after the read has completed? Solution Bytes 3, 4, 5 and 6 of the sequence, i.e. 1, 5, 9, 2. Question 24 Suppose that a 10-MB file is stored on a disk on the same track (track 50) in consecutive sectors. The disk arm is currently situated over track number 100. How long will it take to retrieve this file from the disk? Assume that it takes about 1 ms to move the arm from one cylinder to the next and about 5 ms for the sector where the beginning of the file is stored to rotate under the head. Also, assume that reading occurs at a rate of 200 MB/s. Solution Time to retrieve the file = 50 × 1 ms (time to move the arm over track 50) + 5 ms (time for the first sector to rotate under the head) + (10/200) × 1000 ms (reading 10 MB) = 105 ms Question 25 What is the essential difference between a block special file and a character special file? Solution Block special files model devices made of randomly addressable blocks, such as disks and SSDs: opening one and reading, say, block 4 accesses the fourth block on the device directly, and any block can be sought and read or written independently of all the others. Character special files model devices that produce or accept a pure character stream — printers, keyboards, mice — where seeking is meaningless: bytes are read or written strictly in order. Question 26 In the example making the system call, the library procedure is called read and the system call itself is called read. Is it essential that both of these have the same name? If not, which one is more important? Solution System calls do not really have names, other than in a documentation sense. When the library procedure read traps to the kernel, it puts the number of the system call in a register or on the stack. This number is used to index into a table. There is really no name used anywhere. On the other hand, the name of the library procedure is very important, since that is what appears in the program. Question 27 Modern operating systems decouple a process address space from the machine’s physical memory. List two advantages of this design. Solution This allows an executable program to be loaded in different parts of the machine’s memory in different runs. Also, it enables program size to exceed the size of the machine’s memory. Question 28 To a programmer, a system call looks like any other call to a library procedure. Is it important that a programmer know which library procedures result in system calls? Under what circumstances and why? Solution As far as program logic is concerned, it does not matter whether a call to a library procedure results in a system call. But if performance is an issue, if a task can be accomplished without a system call the program will run faster. Every system call involves overhead time in switching from the user context to the kernel context. Furthermore, on a multi-user system the operating system may schedule another process to run when a system call completes, further slowing the progress in real time of a calling process. Question 29 For each of the calls listed as having no Win32 equivalent, what are the consequences for a programmer of converting a UNIX program to run under Windows? UNIX Win32 Description fork CreateProcess Create a new process waitpid WaitForSingleObject Can wait for a process to exit execve (none) CreateProcess = fork + execve exit ExitProcess Terminate execution open CreateFile Create a file or open an existing file close CloseHandle Close a file read ReadFile Read data from a file write WriteFile Write data to a file lseek SetFilePointer Move the file pointer stat GetFileAttributesEx Get various file attributes mkdir CreateDirectory Create a new directory rmdir RemoveDirectory Remove an empty directory link (none) Win32 does not support links unlink DeleteFile Destroy an existing file mount (none) Win32 does not support mount umount (none) Win32 does not support mount, so no umount chdir SetCurrentDirectory Change the current working directory chmod (none) Win32 does not support security (although NT does) kill (none) Win32 does not support signals time GetLocalTime Get the current time Solution Several UNIX calls have no counterpart in the Win32 API: Link: a Win32 program cannot refer to a file by an alternative name or see it in more than one directory. Also, attempting to create a link is a convenient way to test for and create a lock on a file. Mount and umount: a Windows program cannot make assumptions about standard path names because on systems with multiple disk drives the drive-name part of the path may be different. Chmod: Windows uses access control lists. Kill: Windows programmers cannot kill a misbehaving program that is not cooperating. Question 30 A portable operating system is one that can be ported from one system architecture to another without any modification. Explain why it is infeasible to build an operating system that is completely portable. Describe two high-level layers that you will have in designing an operating system that is highly portable. Solution Every system architecture has its own set of instructions that it can execute. Thus a Pentium cannot execute SPARC programs and a SPARC cannot execute Pentium programs. Also, different architectures differ in bus architecture used (such as VME, ISA, PCI, MCA, SBus, …) as well as the word size of the CPU (usually 32 or 64 bit). Because of these differences in hardware, it is not feasible to build an operating system that is completely portable. A highly portable operating system will consist of two high-level layers — a machine-dependent layer and a machine-independent layer. The machine-dependent layer addresses the specifics of the hardware and must be implemented separately for every architecture. This layer provides a uniform interface on which the machine-independent layer is built. The machine-independent layer has to be implemented only once. To be highly portable, the size of the machine-dependent layer must be kept as small as possible. Question 31 Explain how separation of policy and mechanism aids in building microkernel-based operating systems. Solution Separation of policy and mechanism allows OS designers to implement a small number of basic primitives in the kernel. These primitives are simplified, because they are not dependent on any specific policy. They can then be used to implement more complex mechanisms and policies at the user level. Question 32 Virtual machines have become very popular for a variety of reasons. Nevertheless, they have some downsides. Name one. Solution The virtualization layer costs extra memory and CPU time — privileged operations must be trapped and emulated — so performance drops. Question 33 Here are some questions for practicing unit conversions: How long is a nanoyear in seconds? Micrometers are often called microns. How long is a megamicron? How many bytes are there in a 1-PB memory? The mass of the earth is 6000 yottagrams. What is that in kilograms? Solution The conversions are straightforward: A nanoyear is 10⁻⁹ × 365 × 24 × 3600 = 31.536 ms. 1 meter (10⁶ × 10⁻⁶ m) There are 2⁵⁰ bytes, which is 1,099,511,627,776 bytes. It is 6 × 10²⁴ kg or 6 × 10²⁷ g. Question 34 Write a shell that is similar to the code below but contains enough code that it actually works so you can test it. You might also add some features such as redirection of input and output, pipes, and background jobs. #define TRUE 1 while (TRUE) { /* Main loop: the shell runs forever. */ type_prompt(); /* Print the prompt and wait for input. */ read_command(command, parameters); /* Read one line and split it into command + arguments. */ if (fork() != 0) { /* fork() returns the child's PID, so this branch is the parent. */ /* Parent branch: just wait for the child to finish. */ waitpid(-1, &status, 0); /* Wait for any child process to terminate. */ } else { /* Child branch: replace ourselves with the requested program. */ execve(command, parameters, 0); /* Load and run the command; returns only if it fails. */ } } Throughout this book, TRUE is assumed to be defined as 1. Solution #include <stdio.h> #include <stdlib.h> #define TRUE 1 int main() { while (TRUE) { /* Main loop: the shell never exits on its own. */ type_prompt(); /* Show the prompt. */ read_command(command, parameters); /* Parse the typed line into command + arguments. */ pid_t pid = fork(); /* Create a child process that will run the command. */ if (pid == -1) { printf("Error!\n"); /* fork() failed (e.g. the process table is full). */ exit(-1); } else if (pid > 0) { int status; waitpid(pid, &status, 0); /* Parent: wait for this specific child to finish. */ } else { execve(command, parameters, 0); /* Child: load the requested program. */ exit(1); /* Reached only if execve failed. */ } } return 0; } Question 35 If you have a personal UNIX-like system (Linux, MINIX 3, FreeBSD, etc.) available that you can safely crash and reboot, write a shell script that attempts to create an unlimited number of child processes and observe what happens. Before running the experiment, type sync to the shell to flush the file system buffers to disk to avoid ruining the file system. You can also do the experiment safely in a virtual machine. Note: Do not try this on a shared system without first getting permission from the system administrator. The consequences will be instantly obvious so you are likely to be caught and sanctions may follow. Solution In most UNIX systems you can type ulimit -a to check max user processes. #include <stdio.h> #include <stdlib.h> #define TRUE 1 int main(){ int pid; int max_pid = 0; /* Largest PID observed so far. */ while(TRUE){ pid = fork(); /* Both parent and child keep running after this point. */ max_pid = getpid(); /* Remember our own PID. */ if(pid == 0){ /* Child branch. */ if(max_pid < getpid()) max_pid = getpid(); printf("pid: %d, maximum %d.\n", getpid(), max_pid); return 0; /* The child prints once and exits. */ } else if(pid == -1){ /* fork() failed: no room for more processes. */ printf("Maximum process: %d.\n", max_pid); exit(-1); } /* Parent (pid > 0) loops around and forks again. */ } return 0; } Question 36 Examine and try to interpret the contents of a UNIX-like or Windows directory with a tool like the UNIX od program. (Hint: How you do this will depend upon what the OS allows. One trick that may work is to create a directory on a USB stick with one operating system and then read the raw device data using a different operating system that allows such access.) Solution The tool to display i-node detail for a filesystem will be filesystem specific. For the ext2, ext3, ext4 filesystems (the most common Linux filesystems), you can use debugfs, for XFS xfs_db, for ZFS zdb. For btrfs some information is available using the btrfs command. For example, to explore a directory on an ext4 filesystem (in this case / is dev/sda1): # ls src Animation.js Map.js MarkerCluster.js ScriptsUtil.js Directions.js MapTypeId.js markerclusterer.js TravelMode.js library.js MapUtils.js Polygon.js UnitSystem.js loadScripts.js Marker.js Polyline.js Waypoint.js # ls -lid src 664488 drwxrwxrwx 2 vagrant vagrant 4096 Jul 15 13:24 src # debugfs /dev/sda1 debugfs: imap <664488> Inode 664488 is part of block group 81 located at block 2622042, offset 0x0700 debugfs: dump src src.out debugfs: quit # od -c src.out 0000000 Question 37 (5th edition) What is multiprogramming? Solution Multiprogramming means keeping several jobs in main memory at the same time, each in its own partition. While one job waits for I/O to complete, the CPU runs another job instead of sitting idle, so with enough jobs in memory the expensive CPU can be kept busy nearly 100% of the time. Question 38 (5th edition) What is the purpose of a system call in an operating system? Solution A system call is the interface between user programs and the operating system: a controlled entry point through which a program requests kernel services — using abstractions such as creating, reading, writing and deleting files, as well as resource-management operations. User code cannot touch the hardware directly, so without system calls it could neither use convenient abstractions nor get anything privileged done safely. Question 39 (5th edition) What is the key difference between a trap and an interrupt? Solution A trap is synchronous: it is caused by the running program itself — either deliberately, by executing the trap instruction to request a kernel service, or by a CPU-detected exception such as division by 0 — so it occurs at a predictable point in the instruction stream. An interrupt is asynchronous: it is caused by external hardware, e.g. an I/O device signalling completion, and can arrive between any two instructions, unrelated to what the program is doing. Question 40 (5th edition) Give one reason why mounting file systems is a better design option than prefixing path names with a drive name or number. Explain why file systems are almost always mounted on empty directories. Solution Mounting merges every device into a single directory tree, so paths stay valid no matter which disk holds the files, and removable media can be attached and detached transparently; drive letters bake the device into every path, so everything breaks as soon as files move to another device. File systems are mounted on empty directories because mounting covers up whatever was in the mount point: any files already there become inaccessible while the device is mounted. Question 41 (5th edition) What is spooling? Do you think that advanced personal computers will have spooling as a standard feature in the future? Solution Spooling (Simultaneous Peripheral Operation On Line) means staging jobs on disk first: incoming jobs are read onto the disk as soon as they arrive and output is written to disk for later printing, so slow peripheral work overlaps with computing instead of wasting the expensive machine. Yes — it is standard on personal computers to this day: every modern OS spools printer output through a print queue managed by a daemon for exactly the same reason. Question 42 (5th edition) Why was timesharing not widespread on second-generation computers? Solution Second-generation machines (1955–1965) were multimillion-dollar transistor mainframes locked in machine rooms and run in batch mode: programmers handed card decks to operators and waited for printed output. Timesharing needs many cheap interactive terminals on one machine plus hardware for multiprogramming and memory protection — none of which existed yet; interactive use only became practical with third-generation machines. Question 43 (5th edition) List some differences between personal computer operating systems and mainframe operating systems. Solution Mainframe operating systems serve many simultaneous users with huge I/O capacity, supporting batch, timesharing and transaction processing at once; throughput, reliability and protection of shared data matter most. title: W1. Linear Programming Basics
text: 1. Theory 1.1 Foundations and Core Philosophy of Optimization Optimization is the purposeful discipline and mathematical process of finding the best possible decision—maximizing or minimizing a given quantitative criterion—among a collection of available alternatives, subject to prescribed conditions or restrictions. Formally, an optimization problem seeks an optimal parameter vector within a defined search domain such that: where is the objective function (or cost function), and the feasible domain is delineated by functional constraints and parameter boundaries. The fundamental purpose across science, engineering, operations research, and economics extends far beyond finding a merely valid or feasible solution (any point satisfying the constraints); human intention aims to determine the optimal solution that achieves the absolute extreme of the objective criterion. Why It Matters: Real-world systems—whether allocating production resources, training machine learning models, or routing transport networks—possess scarce resources and competing operational choices. Optimization converts qualitative decision-making into rigorous mathematical formulations, deriving formal criteria for the existence, uniqueness, and computability of peak system performance. The Algorithmic Imperative (Exact vs. Iterative Solvers): A central peculiarity of operations research is that practical models rarely yield closed-form algebraic solutions (explicit “plug-in” formulas). Instead, solutions must be generated by numerical algorithms—prescribed sequences of computational operations executed iteratively: where each iteration attempts to transition the candidate vector closer to the true optimum . Because repetitive algebraic computations over multiple dimensions are tedious and voluminous, modern optimization is inherently computer-assisted. This reliance on iterative algorithms introduces four core computational challenges: Convergence speed: The rate at which the error sequence approaches zero (e.g., linear, superlinear, or quadratic convergence). Numerical precision and error tolerance: Floating-point rounding limits, machine precision, and stopping thresholds . Computational complexity: The scaling of iteration runtimes and memory demands as the number of variables and constraints expands. Algorithmic trapping: Distinguishing between local optima and global extrema depending on model convexity. Heuristic Search Fallback: When mathematical formulations exhibit extreme combinatorial explosion, non-smoothness, or NP-hard computational barriers, finding a provably exact optimum within a feasible timeframe becomes impossible. Under these circumstances, exact algorithms are abandoned in favor of heuristics—intelligent, rule-of-thumb search procedures (such as greedy priority rules, local neighborhood searches, simulated annealing, or genetic algorithms). Heuristics sacrifice theoretical guarantees of absolute optimality to locate acceptable, high-quality, near-optimal solutions within practical computational budgets. Worked Mini-Illustration: Consider choosing an operating parameter to minimize the quadratic operating loss . Closed-form approach: Setting the derivative yields the exact stationary minimum with directly. Iterative gradient step approach: If represents a black-box response evaluated via an iterative update with step size starting from an initial guess : Iteration 1: , reducing loss from to . Iteration 2: , further reducing loss to . Successive algorithmic evaluations generate a sequence converging toward . Key Pitfalls: Confusing feasibility with optimality. A solution is feasible if it merely obeys every system constraint; it is optimal only if no other feasible vector yields a superior objective value. Conversely, assuming that every optimization problem admits a closed-form formula overlooks the inherently algorithmic, iterative nature of computational solvers and the necessity of heuristic approximations when scaling limits are reached. 1.2 Data-Driven Optimization Motivating Examples A data-driven optimization problem is a mathematical formulation where the objective function, constraints, or both are constructed directly from empirical observations, measurements, or network topologies rather than purely theoretical laws. In modern computing, optimization serves as the computational engine for extracting structure, learning representations, and finding optimal discrete configurations from data. Why this matters: across scientific computing, artificial intelligence, and operations research, practical problems rarely arrive as pre-packaged equations. Framing raw data as an optimization problem bridges real-world measurements and rigorous algorithmic solutions. Three fundamental paradigms demonstrate how diverse data models translate into concrete optimization problems: 1.2.1 Least-Squares Linear Regression as Continuous Unconstrained Optimization When fitting an affine-linear model to experimental observations , the goal is to find parameters that best explain the data. For an overdetermined system where (more data points than model parameters), no straight line passes through all points simultaneously, making the linear system inconsistent. The task is formulated as minimizing the squared Euclidean norm of the residual error vector : Geometrically, this is an orthogonal projection of the measurement vector onto the column space of , denoted . The error vector must be orthogonal to every column of , leading directly to the normal equations: Worked Illustration: Consider three experimental measurements: at , at , and at . If the line passed through all three points, it would satisfy: Because these three points are not collinear, has no exact solution. Formulating the normal equations: Solving the system: The unique least-squares optimal affine model is . Evaluating this fitted line at the sample times produces the projection vector , which minimizes the total sum of squared residuals . 1.2.2 Training Artificial Neural Networks as Parameter Misfit Minimization In supervised machine learning, an artificial neural network models an unknown target relationship using a parameterized network architecture. Given a training dataset with feature vectors and corresponding target labels , a single artificial neuron computes a linear combination of its inputs shifted by a scalar bias , which is then passed through an activation function : where denotes the synaptic weights. Training the neuron corresponds to an unconstrained continuous optimization problem: adjust decision vector to minimize a scalar misfit objective function over all training samples: where is a loss metric (such as squared error ). In realistic multi-layer perceptrons, this principle extends directly: the model becomes a deep concatenation of alternating linear transfers and nonlinear activations, resulting in a highly non-convex, high-dimensional parameter optimization problem solved via iterative gradient algorithms. 1.2.3 Traveling Salesperson Problem (TSP) as Combinatorial Graph Optimization Unlike regression and neural network training where decision variables live in continuous spaces ( ), network routing problems operate on discrete combinatorial structures. In the Traveling Salesperson Problem (TSP), given a set of vertices (cities) connected by edges with associated non-negative weights (such as flight airfares, distances, or transit times), the goal is to find a closed tour (Hamiltonian cycle) that visits every city exactly once and returns to the departure city with the minimum total cost: subject to: Each city is entered exactly once. Each city is exited exactly once. Subtours (disconnected sub-cycles that do not span all vertices) are strictly eliminated. Conceptual Example (Airfare Routing): Given a complete network of five cities—San Francisco, Los Angeles, Denver, Detroit, New York—with known pairwise non-directional airfares (e.g., San Francisco–Los Angeles: , San Francisco–Denver: , San Francisco–Detroit: , Detroit–New York: , etc.), solving the TSP requires searching the discrete permutations of vertices to select the cycle minimizing total ticket price. 1.2.4 Pitfalls and Typical Confusions Exact Solvability vs. Best Approximation: A frequent mistake when handling inconsistent systems is attempting to find a vector satisfying . In overdetermined data problems, an exact solution does not exist; optimization defines what “best” means (e.g., minimizing squared Euclidean error via ) rather than solving an exact linear system. Continuous vs. Combinatorial Complexity: In continuous unconstrained convex problems like least squares, the global optimum can often be expressed analytically via normal equations or reached reliably via gradients. In discrete combinatorial problems like TSP, the solution space grows factorially ( undirected tours for cities), rendering brute-force enumeration impossible for large instances and necessitating specialized integer programming formulations or heuristics. 1.3 Problem Anatomy, Decision Frameworks, and Operations Research Phases Every mathematical optimization model rests on three foundational pillars: 1. Decision alternatives (or decision variables): Controllable quantities whose values the decision-maker selects. 2. Constraints: Restrictions, physical limits, or operational demands that dictate which values of are permissible, expressed as inequalities ( ) and equalities ( ). 3. Objective criterion (or objective function): An evaluative metric that maps candidate decisions to a scalar value to be minimized or maximized. A candidate decision is a feasible solution if it satisfies every constraint simultaneously: for all , for all , and . The collection of all such points forms the feasible set (or feasible solution space), denoted by . A model is infeasible if its feasible set is empty ( ). A solution is an optimal solution if for all in a minimization problem (or in a maximization problem). A mathematical program is called solvable if it admits at least one optimal solution. ┌─────────────────────────┐ │ Decision Alternatives │ │ x ∈ D ⊆ Rⁿ │ └────────────┬────────────┘ │ ┌───────────────┴───────────────┐ ▼ ▼ ┌───────────────────┐ ┌───────────────────┐ │ Constraints │ │Objective Criterion│ │ g(x) ≤ 0, l(x) = 0│ │ min/max f(x) │ └─────────┬─────────┘ └─────────┬─────────┘ │ │ ▼ │ ┌───────────────────┐ │ │ Feasible Set │ │ │ x ∈ F ⊆ Rⁿ │ │ └─────────┬─────────┘ │ │ │ └───────────────┬───────────────┘ ▼ ┌─────────────────────────┐ │ Optimal Solution │ │ x* ∈ F: best f(x*) │ └─────────────────────────┘ 1.3.1 Operations Research Method Taxonomy Operations Research (OR) does not rely on a single monolithic algorithm. Methods are classified into four broad methodological branches: Mathematical programming: Techniques to optimize a function subject to deterministic constraints. Subdivided by structure into calculus and variational methods, linear programming (LP), integer programming (IP), dynamic programming (DP), nonlinear programming (NLP), quadratic programming (QP), network methods, and game theory. Stochastic process techniques: Methods for analyzing systems governed by probabilistic mechanisms and random variables, including Markov processes, queueing theory, renewal theory, reliability theory, and simulation models. Statistical methods: Empirical modeling and inference strategies, including linear and nonlinear regression, cluster analysis, discriminant analysis, and design of experiments (DoE). Modern or nontraditional optimization techniques: Metaheuristics and nature-inspired algorithms developed for complex, non-convex, or NP-hard landscapes where exact algorithms stall, including genetic algorithms (GA), simulated annealing (SA), particle swarm optimization (PSO), ant colony optimization (ACO), neural networks, and fuzzy optimization. 1.3.2 The Five Phases of an Operations Research Study Translating a real-world dilemma into operational practice follows five sequential phases: 1. Problem definition: Identifying the system boundaries, relevant stakeholders, resource limits, decision alternatives, and the primary objective criterion. 2. Model construction: Translating verbal descriptions and empirical measurements into mathematical functions, equations, and sets ( , , ). 3. Model solution: Applying exact mathematical programming algorithms or heuristics to compute optimal or near-optimal decisions . This third phase is the best-defined and mathematically most tractable phase of an OR project, as it operates on formal, self-contained equations. 4. Model validation: Testing whether the mathematical abstraction represents the real system with sufficient fidelity (e.g., verifying against historical data and stress-testing edge cases). 5. Implementation: Translating algorithmic outputs into standard operating procedures, software workflows, and operational decision rules. Phases 1, 2, 4, and 5 represent an interactive human art rather than pure closed-form theory. 1.3.3 Worked Illustration: Multi-Week Ticket Purchasing Problem A businessperson has a 5-week recurring commitment requiring travel from Kazan (KZN) to Moscow (MOS), departing KZN every Monday morning and returning from MOS every Wednesday afternoon. The airline pricing schedule is: Regular roundtrip ticket: . Weekend-spanning roundtrip ticket: discount . One-way ticket (either direction): of regular roundtrip price . Decision Problem Formulation: Alternatives: Discrete ticket-purchasing schedules spanning the 5-week horizon. Constraint: The traveler must depart KZN on Monday and return on Wednesday of the exact same week for each of the 5 consecutive weeks. Objective criterion: Minimize total purchasing expenditure. Evaluation of Discrete Strategies: Alternative 1 (Independent weekly tickets): Purchase 5 standard same-week roundtrips (KZN–MOS–KZN). None span a weekend. Alternative 2 (One-way boundaries + reverse weekend roundtrips): Purchase one one-way KZN MOS on Monday of Week 1, four weekend-spanning roundtrips originating in Moscow (MOS–KZN–MOS) covering Wednesdays of Week to Mondays of Week ( ), and one final one-way MOS KZN on Wednesday of Week 5: Alternative 3 (Staggered weekend-spanning tickets): Purchase one KZN–MOS–KZN roundtrip ticket departing Monday of Week 1 and returning Wednesday of Week 5 (spanning 4 weekends; cost ). Cover the intermediate trips using four nested MOS–KZN–MOS roundtrip tickets departing Wednesday of Week and returning Monday of Week for (each spanning one weekend; cost each). All 5 purchased tickets span at least one weekend: Every alternative satisfies the operational calendar restriction ( ), making all three feasible. Because , Alternative 3 is the unique optimal solution, achieving an expenditure of . 1.3.4 Pitfalls and Conceptual Distinctions Closed-Form Formulas vs. Iterative Algorithms: Unlike elementary calculus problems where unconstrained optima are computed by setting derivatives directly to zero ( ) and solving algebraically, OR models generally lack closed-form solutions. They require iterative algorithms that systematically generate a sequence of points moving monotonically toward the optimum. Model Infeasibility vs. Algorithm Failure: An empty feasible set ( ) is an intrinsic structural property of mutually contradictory constraints (e.g., and ), not a failure of the numerical solver. If a problem is infeasible, no optimal solution exists. Mathematical Optimality vs. Practical Fidelity: An algorithmically optimal solution optimizes only the specific mathematical formulation provided. If Phase 1 (definition) or Phase 2 (construction) omits latent real-world constraints, may prove practically unworkable or sub-optimal in Phase 5. 1.4 Mathematical Programming Formulations and Problem Taxonomies A general constrained mathematical programming problem is defined as finding a decision vector that minimizes an objective function (or cost function) over a prescribed feasible domain: where are inequality constraints, are equality constraints, and denotes the underlying ground set. The number of variables and the constraint counts and are independent. When and , the problem becomes an unconstrained optimization problem: Problems are categorized primarily by their decision domain : Continuous Optimization: The domain is a continuum, such as the full space , a box domain , or a unit simplex . The functions are typically continuous or differentiable over . Discrete (Combinatorial) Optimization: The domain consists of discrete, isolated points, such as the integer lattice or binary vectors . Within continuous optimization, structure dictates solvability: Linear Optimization (LO / LP): The domain is , and all functions , , and are strictly affine (linear combinations of variables plus a constant). Convex Optimization: The ground set is convex, each equality constraint is affine, and the objective as well as all inequality constraints are convex functions, satisfying the Jensen-type inequality: Nonlinear Continuous Optimization: At least one of the objective or constraint functions contains nonlinear terms that fail convexity or affine requirements. 1.4.1 The Representation Criterion Optimization taxonomy adheres to the representation criterion: a problem’s class is strictly determined by how its mathematical model is explicitly formulated, not by any equivalent problem into which it could hypothetically be transformed. Nonlinear vs. Linear Representation: Although the constraint system is purely linear and is strictly monotonic (meaning minimizing yields the exact same minimizer as minimizing ), this model is not a linear program. The objective expression is nonlinear; hence, as presented, it belongs to nonlinear continuous optimization. Finite vs. Semi-Infinite Representation: Even though every single constraint is affine, the index set generates an infinite family of constraints. A standard linear programming model requires a finite constraint index ( ). Consequently, this formulation is classified as a semi-infinite programming problem rather than a standard linear program. 1.4.2 Why Problem Taxonomy Matters Algorithm design depends entirely on taxonomy: linear programs admit finite polynomial-time interior point methods and vertex-hopping simplex pivots; convex problems guarantee that any local minimum is a global minimum; and discrete combinatorial problems often require branch-and-bound or cutting-plane routines due to NP-hardness. Misclassifying an analytical model risks deploying algorithms whose convergence guarantees do not apply. 1.4.3 Worked Illustration Consider classifying the following two formulations: Formulation A: Classification: is convex ( ), and is affine (thus convex). The domain is (continuous). This is a linearly constrained convex quadratic program (a subfield of continuous convex optimization). Formulation B: Classification: The objective and constraint functions are linear, but the variable domain is . Because the domain is non-continuous, it is classified as a binary integer linear program (combinatorial optimization), not a continuous linear program. 1.4.4 Common Pitfalls Confusing Equivalent Solutions with Equivalent Problem Classes: Transforming an objective via a monotonic transformation (e.g., replacing with ) produces identical optimal points , but the first is non-differentiable at zero while the second is a smooth quadratic program. Taxonomy applies strictly to the written algebraic form. Assuming Linear Constraints Imply a Linear Program: A problem where all constraints are linear hyperplanes is still classified as nonlinear if the objective contains powers, products of variables, or transcendental functions. Overlooking Constraint Cardinality: Linearity of every individual constraint function is insufficient if the constraint index set is unbounded; infinite sets of linear inequalities define semi-infinite programs, which require specialized functional-analytic solution methods. 1.5 Linear Programming Modeling and Canonical Equivalence Transformations A linear programming (LP) problem (or linear optimization problem) is a mathematical program whose objective function and all functional constraints are affine (linear) expressions of continuous decision variables over a finite constraint index set: Linearly constrained problems with nonlinear terms (such as or ) or with an infinite collection of constraints (such as for all integers ) violate this definition and cannot be processed by standard linear programming algorithms. Furthermore, an optimization problem is categorized as an LP strictly based on its explicit formulation, not on whether a nonlinear presentation might be indirectly transformed into one. 1.5.1 Why Canonical Form Matters Theoretical algorithms (such as the simplex tableau, interior-point methods, and duality theory) assume a single, standardized mathematical structure. Expressing every problem in a unified format—the canonical maximization form—eliminates edge cases in algorithm design, proves general duality theorems, and enables general-purpose matrix solvers. 1.5.2 Canonical Representation Formats In canonical form, the goal is always maximization, and all functional constraints are expressed as “ ” inequalities: 1. Forgetting to negate introduces false boundaries. Implicit Non-Negativity: Real-world quantities (such as tons of paint or pounds of feed) cannot be negative. Omitting allows solvers to generate economically meaningless solutions where unconstrained negative production generates artificial profits or satisfies blending requirements. 1.6 Graphical Solution Method and Geometric Outcomes in 2D The graphical solution method is a visual, geometric technique used to solve two-variable linear programs ( ).
