title: W2. Philosophy of AI
text: 1. Theory 1.1 Epistemology and the Definition of Knowledge Epistemology is the branch of philosophy concerned with the nature, sources, and limits of knowledge—derived from the Greek epistēmē (ἐπιστήμη, “knowledge”) and logos (λόγος, “logical discourse” or “study”). It asks the foundational question: how do we know what we know? In classical philosophy, the standard analytical framework traced to Socrates defines knowledge through the tripartite definition, commonly abbreviated as Justified True Belief (JTB). Under this formulation, a cognitive agent or subject possesses knowledge of a proposition ( ) if and only if three distinct conditions are satisfied simultaneously: Truth: The proposition corresponds to objective reality. Truth is independent of an observer’s internal state: if is objectively false, it cannot be known. Belief: The subject accepts as true; it represents the subjective mental representation or internal stance toward reality. One cannot know a fact without believing it. Justification: The subject possesses an adequate rational explanation, evidence, or epistemic grounding supporting . A mere arbitrary guess that happens to be right does not qualify. Formally: Why it matters: Artificial intelligence systems—from symbolic knowledge bases and theorem provers to modern neural models—manipulate representations of the world. To assess whether an artificial system truly possesses “knowledge” rather than superficial pattern matching or statistical guessing, we require a formal benchmark separating mere stored data or lucky predictions from epistemically grounded representations. 1.1.1 The Gettier Problem: Accidental Truth For centuries, JTB was regarded as providing the necessary and sufficient conditions for knowledge. In 1963, American philosopher Edmund Gettier published a landmark paper demonstrating that JTB is insufficient: an agent can hold a justified belief that happens to be true entirely by luck or accident, without possessing genuine knowledge. The Smith and Jones Thought Experiment (Gettier, 1963): Two applicants, Smith and Jones, apply for a job. Smith has strong evidence for two premises: the company director assured him that Jones would be chosen, and Smith personally counted 10 coins in Jones’s pocket moments earlier. From these premises, Smith logically deduces the proposition : “The man who will get the job has 10 coins in his pocket.” Smith accepts (Belief), and his belief is supported by reliable testimony and direct count (Justification). In an unexpected reversal, the director hires Smith instead of Jones. Furthermore, entirely unknown to Smith, Smith himself happens to carry exactly 10 coins in his own pocket. Analysis: Proposition is objectively true (Truth); Smith explicitly believes (Belief); and Smith arrived at via valid deduction from credible evidence (Justification). However, Smith clearly did not know —the proposition was made true by a state of affairs (Smith’s coins and Smith’s hiring) completely disconnected from the justification he relied upon (Jones’s coins and Jones’s hiring). His justification proceeded via a justified false belief. The Epistemological Lesson: Justification must be non-accidentally and properly connected to the truth. In AI, this distinction is critical: a predictive model may produce a correct output from an unsound intermediate feature or spurious correlation; while the output is true and nominally justified by its training loss, the system lacks grounded epistemic knowledge. Key Pitfalls: Confusing belief with knowledge: High certainty or probabilistic model confidence is purely subjective; confidence alone never converts an ungrounded or false statement into knowledge. Assuming justification implies truth: An agent can be completely rational, methodologically sound, and fully justified in believing a falsehood (as Smith was regarding Jones’s hiring). Treating JTB as sufficient: Accidental alignment between evidence and reality satisfies JTB mechanically while failing the requirement of genuine epistemic grounding. 1.2 The Turing Test and Operational Intelligence The Turing Test is an operational definition of machine intelligence proposed by British mathematician Alan Mathison Turing in his seminal 1950 Mind paper, “Computing Machinery and Intelligence.” Instead of debating the subjective, metaphysical question “Can machines think?”, Turing reformulated the inquiry into an empirical criterion of behavioral indistinguishability: can a digital computer successfully imitate human verbal behavior under blind testing conditions? +------------------+ Teletype Link A +-------------------+ | | <=============================> | Hidden Entity A | | Human | | (Human or Machine)| | Interrogator (C) | Teletype Link B +-------------------+ | | <=============================> | Hidden Entity B | +------------------+ | (Machine or Human)| +-------------------+ 1.2.1 Turing’s Contributions and Historical Context Turing’s formulation of operational intelligence built upon foundational milestones in mathematical logic and computing: Universal Turing Machine (UTM) and the Church–Turing Thesis: Formulated during his fellowship at King’s College, Cambridge, proving that a simple abstract machine manipulating discrete symbols on an infinite tape can simulate any algorithmic computation. Turing later completed his PhD at Princeton, declining John von Neumann’s postdoctoral offer to return to Cambridge. Cryptanalysis at Bletchley Park: During World War II, Turing designed the electromechanical Bombe decoder to break the German Enigma cipher. His technical monographs (The Applications of Probability to Cryptography and Paper on Statistics of Repetitions) remained classified by the British government for roughly 70 years. Persecution and Legacy: Despite pioneering artificial intelligence, computer design, and mathematical biology, Turing was criminally prosecuted for homosexuality by the UK government in 1952, leading to chemical castration. He died of cyanide poisoning in 1954. He received an official government apology in 2009 and a royal pardon in 2013. 1.2.2 The Imitation Game Protocol Turing framed the benchmark as the Imitation Game: 1. Setup: Three participants are isolated in separate rooms: a human interrogator ( ), a hidden human ( ), and a hidden machine ( ) running an automated agent. 2. Channel: Communication occurs solely via neutral text interfaces (originally a teletype, avoiding clues from vocal tone, physical appearance, or sensory capabilities). 3. Objective: Interrogator submits arbitrary questions to both entities. Entity (the machine) attempts to deceive into believing it is the human, while entity attempts to assist in making the correct identification. 4. Decision Metric: Let be the probability that interrogator misidentifies the machine as the human. If when testing the machine is statistically comparable to the rate at which an interrogator misidentifies a human playing against another human, the machine has passed the test. 1.2.3 Domain Limitations and Operationalism The standard Turing Test operates as an external behavioral test: it evaluates input-output functional equivalence rather than underlying cognitive architecture or conscious awareness. * Narrow vs. Broad Domains: While early systems achieved conversational mimicry in restricted domains or through scripted evasions, open-ended conversational coherence across arbitrary common-sense reasoning, humor, and episodic context remains an elusive benchmark for general intelligence. * Asymmetric Competence: The test penalizes machines for super-human capabilities. A system that instantly calculates reveals its artificial identity unless it deliberately delays its response or injects arithmetic errors to simulate human cognitive latency. 1.2.4 The Inverse Turing Test: CAPTCHA When the roles of the interrogator and respondent are reversed such that an automated system interrogates an unseen user, the protocol becomes an Inverse Turing Test. This is implemented globally as CAPTCHA (Completely Automated Public Turing test to tell Computers and Humans Apart). * Purpose: Provides a computationally cheap, cost-effective defense against automated bots in web workflows: preventing spam in account creation, securing online ordering queues, and protecting email registrations. * Modalities: 1. Distorted Text and OCR: Systems such as early reCAPTCHA presented pairs of distorted character strings (e.g., "Mills," alongside scanned book snippets "sposcz"). The system leveraged human perceptual processing to decipher optical character recognition (OCR) failures encountered during the digitization of physical archives. 2. Image-Grid Classification: Challenges presenting a visual array requiring the user to select all cells containing specific target objects (e.g., “Select all squares with traffic lights”). 3. Audio Challenges: Phonetically distorted spoken words overlaid with ambient noise, serving as accessibility alternatives while resisting automated speech-to-text parsers. 1.2.5 Worked Mini-Illustration: Evaluating an Interrogation Transcript An interrogator submits a compound prompt over a teletype link: Candidate Machine Model 1 (Raw Compute Engine): Response: "52321. Liquid cellulose interaction causes hydrogen bond degradation." Interrogator Decision: Instantly flagged as machine. Response latency was with immediate exact arithmetic and mechanical prose. Candidate Machine Model 2 (Turing Imitation Strategy): Response (delivered after a pause): "That's around 52,000—52,321 if my mental math holds. As for coffee, the paper fibers soak up the water and swell, and the brown pigments stay behind when it dries, leaving it warped and stained." Interrogator Decision: Indistinguishable from an educated human respondent. The system successfully simulated human response pacing, approximation, and pragmatic discourse. 1.2.6 Common Pitfalls Conflating Operational Indistinguishability with Consciousness: The Turing Test determines whether a system can replicate the external linguistic performance of a human. It does not measure internal semantic understanding, subjective experience (qualia), or sentience. Passing the test satisfies operational behavioral criteria, not philosophical proof of a mind. Confusing Standard Turing Tests with CAPTCHA Directionality: In Turing’s original Imitation Game, a human interrogator evaluates an unknown entity to detect a machine. In a CAPTCHA, a machine algorithm automatically interrogates an unknown remote client to detect whether it is a human. 1.3 Syntax, Semantics, and the Chinese Room Argument The distinction between syntactic manipulation and semantic comprehension forms the primary philosophical boundary between simulation and true cognition in artificial intelligence. Syntax refers to the formal, structural rules governing the arrangement, combination, and transformation of symbols without regard to their interpretation. Semantics refers to the meaning, reference, truth conditions, and intentionality underlying those symbols—connecting representations to the actual objects, relations, and concepts they denote. Strong AI posits that an appropriately programmed computer does not merely simulate a mind, but literally possesses a mind, consciousness, and genuine understanding. In contrast, Weak AI claims only that computational models are powerful tools for studying cognition and automating intelligent tasks. Input (Chinese Characters) │ ▼ [In Slot] ┌───────────────────────────┐ │ The Chinese Room │ │ ┌─────────────────────┐ │ │ │ English Speaker │ │ │ │ (No Chinese) │ │ │ └──────────┬──────────┘ │ │ │ consults │ │ ┌──────────▼──────────┐ │ │ │ Formal Rulebook │ │ │ │ (If "漢" then "語") │ │ │ └─────────────────────┘ │ └─────────┬─────────────────┘ ▼ [Out Slot] Output (Chinese Characters) 1.3.1 The Thought Experiment and the Critique of Strong AI In 1980, philosopher John Searle introduced the Chinese Room argument to demonstrate that passing an operational assessment such as the Turing Test does not imply genuine mental states or semantic understanding. The setup is defined as follows: 1. An English-speaking human agent who understands zero Chinese is locked inside an isolated room. 2. Batches of Chinese characters are fed into the room through an in slot. 3. The room contains a comprehensive rulebook written entirely in English. The book provides purely formal instructions: when a specific sequence of symbols is matched, look up the corresponding rule and produce another sequence of characters. 4. The agent executes these lookups, writes the resulting characters onto paper, and passes them out through an out slot. To an external native Chinese speaker, the room responds fluently and coherently, effortlessly passing an imitation game. Yet, the human inside does not understand a single word of Chinese; they are executing formal symbol manipulations based strictly on shape and syntax. Searle argues that digital computers operate identically: a central processor manipulates bits according to program instructions (syntax) without any intrinsic grasp of what those bits represent (semantics). Therefore, syntax does not suffice for semantics, and behavioural equivalence does not entail intentionality or comprehension. 1.3.2 Counterarguments and Computational Responses Searle’s thought experiment prompted several key rebuttals: The Systems Reply: While the individual human clerk does not understand Chinese, the entire system—comprising the human, the rulebook, the scratch paper, and the input/output protocol—does instantiate understanding. Cognition is an emergent property of the distributed architecture, much like an individual biological neuron does not understand language, but the human brain as a whole does. External Grounding (The Robot Reply): If the rulebook and processor are placed inside a physical robot equipped with sensors (cameras, microphones) and actuators (manipulators, wheels), the internal symbols become causally linked to physical reality. This interaction grounds abstract syntax in real-world perceptual experience. Rule Induction and Machine Learning: Searle assumed a static, manually hard-coded rulebook written by an external designer (“Who writes the rulebook?”). Modern AI architectures derive and optimize their own latent representations directly from raw data via continuous mathematical optimization, complicating the view that machines are merely static lookup tables. 1.3.3 The Computer Perception Pipeline vs. Conceptualization The semantic gap is evident in how machine vision bridges low-level sensory signals and high-level human categories. Processing an object follows a four-stage cognitive pipeline: Segmentation: Partitioning raw digital images into distinct pixel masks corresponding to continuous surfaces or objects. Detection: Localizing candidate objects within coordinate bounding boxes and assigning probability scores across candidate labels. Conceptualization: Mapping perceptual features into an invariant functional schema. Verbalization: Emitting linguistic tokens that denote the classified concept to external agents. Mini-Illustration: Consider the concept of a chair. In human semantics, a chair is conceptually defined by its functional affordance: “a piece of furniture designed to support a seated human.” Visually, the category spans radical morphological variations: A classical upholstered dark grey armchair with wooden legs; A minimalist slatted wooden upright dining chair; A plush, bright orange children’s armchair shaped like a cartoon tiger; A modern chrome-stemmed height-adjustable swivel bar stool. A standard object detector treats these instances as distinct pixel distributions, running mathematical filters across arrays to match syntax (edges, textures, spatial convolutions). If the model labels all four as chair, it does so by associating statistical patterns with a character string, not by understanding rest, seating, or bodily posture. Key Pitfall: Do not confuse internal functional correctness with semantic comprehension. An AI system that generates grammatically flawless and contextually accurate replies is manipulating high-dimensional representations according to statistical and formal constraints; this operational competence does not settle whether the machine possesses intentionality or subjective awareness. 1.4 Robot Ethics and Asimov’s Laws Normative robot ethics formalizes the moral, legal, and operational constraints governing autonomous physical agents. Isaac Asimov originally structured machine morality around the Three Laws of Robotics, organized as a strict lexicographic priority hierarchy: 1. First Law (Non-maleficence): A robot may not injure a human being or, through inaction, allow a human being to come to harm. 2. Second Law (Obedience): A robot must obey the orders given to it by human beings, except where such orders would conflict with the First Law. 3. Third Law (Self-preservation): A robot must protect its own existence as long as such protection does not conflict with the First or Second Law. To address existential and collective dilemmas, Asimov later introduced the Zeroth Law: Zeroth Law (Collective preservation): A robot may not injure humanity, or, through inaction, allow humanity to come to harm. The Zeroth Law precedes the First Law, modifying it to: “A robot may not injure a human being, unless this conflicts with the Zeroth Law.” This elevation shifts the framework from deontological, individual-level rights to a utilitarian ethical calculus, requiring an agent to weigh individual harm against aggregate existential risk to the human species. ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Zeroth Law │ │ Preserve Humanity (Utilitarian macro-calculus) │ └───────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────┘ │ overrides ┌───────────────────────────▼────────────────────────────┐ │ First Law │ │ Do Not Harm Individual Humans (Deontological) │ └───────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────┘ │ overrides ┌───────────────────────────▼────────────────────────────┐ │ Second Law │ │ Obey Human Orders (Subservience) │ └───────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────┘ │ overrides ┌───────────────────────────▼────────────────────────────┘ │ Third Law │ │ Preserve Own Existence (Self-defense) │ └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ Why it matters: Asimov’s laws expose the limits of high-level rule-based morality. In practice, robots cannot rely on vague natural-language directives (“harm”, “humanity”) without rigorous mathematical definitions of cost, utility, and uncertainty. Modern roboticists separate ethical governance into physical hardware safety envelopes for industry and legal-normative frameworks for lethal tactical systems. 1.4.1 Industrial and Collaborative Physical Safety Traditional factory robotics guarantees the First Law not through reasoning algorithms, but through deterministic spatial isolation: Industrial caged cells: Heavy high-speed manipulators operate behind rigid metal enclosures. Mechanical interlocks cut actuator power immediately if an access gate opens. Safety mats: Pressure-sensitive floor mats placed in human access zones (Zone 1, Zone 2) register worker weight and trigger emergency stops before the manipulator can sweep through the sector. Light curtains and muting sensors: Optical light curtains project arrays of infrared beams across open workstation boundaries; breaking any beam interrupts the safety circuit. Muting sensors temporarily suppress this trip condition only when an expected, identifiable object (such as a pallet on a conveyor) crosses the boundary, distinguishing materials from humans. Collaborative robots (cobots): Modern systems (such as the dual-armed Rethink Robotics Baxter) replace strict physical isolation with power-and-force limiting, rounded compliant joints, integrated torque sensors, and dynamic vision systems that continuously adjust speed and separation margins when humans enter their shared workspace. 1.4.2 Tactical, Police, and Military Autonomous Systems When robots operate outside factory cages, legal and operational doctrines replace fictional constraints: Semi-autonomous combat drones: Military uninhabited aerial vehicles (UAVs) conduct surveillance and deliver precision-guided munitions (e.g., Hellfire missiles). Under international humanitarian law (specifically the Geneva Conventions and the Law of Armed Conflict), targeting decisions require distinction, proportionality, and military necessity, typically mediated via human-in-the-loop or human-on-the-loop command architectures. Municipal tactical robotics: Civil law enforcement operates under constitutional use-of-force standards (e.g., the Fourth Amendment objective reasonableness standard in the US). In the 2016 Dallas police standoff, authorities strapped an explosive payload (detonation cord with C4) to the manipulator arm of an existing Remotec Andros F6A bomb-disposal robot to neutralize an active sniper who had killed five police officers and was barricaded behind cover. This marked the first documented lethal deployment of a domestic police robot in US history, illustrating how human commanders treat robotic platforms as remotely operated lethal tools rather than autonomous moral agents. 1.4.3 Worked Mini-Illustration: Lexicographic Priority vs. Utilitarian Calculus Consider an autonomous perimeter rover evaluating three available actions : Action Impact on Human A Impact on Humanity Human Order Compliance Robot Integrity Harmed ( ) Threat neutralized ( ) Disobeys order ( ) Intact ( ) Unharmed ( ) Threat detonates ( ) Obeys order ( ) Intact ( ) Unharmed ( ) Threat neutralized ( ) Disobeys order ( ) Destroyed ( ) Under the Strict Three Laws (No Zeroth Law): Actions must satisfy first. Action violates Law 1 and is rejected. Between and , both satisfy Law 1 ( ). Law 2 requires obedience ( ). Action is selected, even though it results in catastrophic collective harm ( ). Under the Zeroth Law Hierarchy: Maximize first. Action is eliminated ( ). Between and , both achieve . Applying Law 1 eliminates because . Applying Law 3 to permits the robot to sacrifice itself ( ) because protecting its existence is strictly subordinate to Law 1 and the Zeroth Law. Action is executed. Key Pitfalls: Literary trope vs. engineering architecture: Asimov designed the Three Laws deliberately to fail in complex situations, demonstrating that natural language cannot resolve semantic boundary conflicts (e.g., what constitutes “inaction” or psychological “harm”). Engineers do not program Asimov’s laws; they program objective loss functions, deterministic state machines, and hardware fail-safes. Zeroth Law paternalism: The Zeroth Law transforms an agent into a utilitarian maximizer. Because “humanity” is an abstraction, an autonomous system guided purely by aggregate species utility can justify harm, surveillance, or subjugation of individual humans whenever its internal model predicts a net positive macro-outcome. 1.5 Propositional Logic: Propositions, Connectives, and Truth Tables A proposition is a declarative statement that evaluates to strictly one truth value: either True ( or ) or False ( or ) in classical bivalent logic, but never both simultaneously. A statement that can be assigned a truth value is called an atomic proposition (or propositional variable, typically denoted by lowercase Roman letters ). Expressions that fail this criterion are not propositions: Imperative commands: Statements that instruct action rather than declare fact (e.g., “Open the window.”). Interrogatives: Inquiries seeking information (e.g., “Is the server running?”). Open expressions with free variables: Statements containing unbound variables whose truth value cannot be determined in isolation without contextual binding or values (e.g., “x + 3 = 5”). A false statement (e.g., “7 is an even number”) is still a valid proposition because its truth value is definitively . Why it matters: Symbolic logic provides AI systems with an unambiguous mathematical language for knowledge representation, automated theorem proving, and deterministic decision-making, stripping away natural language ambiguities. 1.5.1 Logical Connectives and Truth Conditions Compound propositions are constructed by joining atomic propositions using formal logical connectives (operators): Negation ( , “NOT ”): A unary operator that inverts the truth value of its operand. is if is , and if is . Conjunction ( , “ AND ”): A binary operator that evaluates to if and only if both and are ; otherwise, it is . Disjunction ( , “ OR ”): The standard logical OR is inclusive disjunction. evaluates to if at least one operand is , evaluating to only when both and are . Exclusive Disjunction ( , “XOR”): Evaluates to if strictly one operand is and the other is . When both operands share identical truth values ( or ), evaluates to . Conditional ( , “Material Implication”): Interpreted as “if , then ”. Here, is the antecedent (hypothesis) and is the consequent (conclusion). The conditional is defined as false in exactly one scenario: when the antecedent is and the consequent is . If is , the implication is automatically regardless of the truth value of —a property known as vacuous truth. “ if ” translates to . “ only if ” translates to . Biconditional ( , “Equivalence” or “IFF”): Interpreted as “p if and only if q”. Evaluates to if and only if both and share the identical truth value (both or both ). For a compound formula comprising distinct propositional variables, the systematic truth table requires exactly distinct rows to cover all combinations of truth assignments. In formal logic, material implication requires no causal connection. Consider: “If the Moon is made of cheese ( ), then ( ).” Because the antecedent is false, the formula evaluates formally to True. “Only If” vs. “If”: In natural language, students frequently reverse the direction of implication. “You enter the lab ( ) if you have an access card ( )” means . In contrast, “You enter the lab ( ) only if you have an access card ( )” establishes that having a card is a necessary condition for entering, translating to . Inclusive vs. Exclusive Disjunction: In natural language, “or” is frequently used exclusively (e.g., “You can have tea or coffee” implies not both). In mathematical logic, without qualification is strictly inclusive: . The exclusive interpretation must be designated explicitly as . 1.6 Propositional Reasoning: Equivalences, Conditional Forms, and Satisfiability A formula’s semantic status depends on how its truth value behaves across the space of all possible truth assignments (models). Propositional reasoning formalizes this behavior to establish semantic validity, test satisfiability, and verify equivalence algebraically without exhaustively calculating rows in truth tables. 1.6.1 Semantic Classification and Satisfiability Every well-formed propositional formula falls into one of three semantic categories: A tautology is a formula that evaluates to true under every possible truth assignment. Formally, for a formula , for all models (written ). A minimal example is the law of excluded middle: . A contradiction (or unsatisfiable formula) is a formula that evaluates to false under every possible truth assignment. Formally, for every model . A minimal example is . A contingency is a formula that evaluates to true under at least one truth assignment and false under at least one other (e.g., , which is true when both atoms are true, but false under any assignment setting either atom to false). Satisfiability characterizes whether a formula has at least one model. A formula is satisfiable if and only if there exists at least one truth assignment under which it evaluates to true. Automated reasoning and constraint satisfaction in AI often reduce planning and verification problems to propositional satisfiability (SAT): deciding whether an assignment exists that satisfies a conjunction of constraints. 1.6.2 Conditional Transformations Given a directed implication (where is the hypothesis/antecedent and is the conclusion/consequent), three related conditional statements can be formed: Converse: (swaps antecedent and consequent). Inverse: (negates both antecedent and consequent). Contrapositive: (negates and swaps both). title: W1. System Modes and Memory
text: 1. Theory 1.1 What Is an Operating System An operating system (OS) is the layer of software between application programs and the bare hardware. It has two complementary jobs, and every exam question about “what the OS does” reduces to one of them. Top-down, the OS is an extended machine. Real hardware is complicated and inconsistent: disks, network cards and printers all speak different low-level protocols. The OS hides this mess behind clean abstractions — files instead of disk blocks, sockets instead of wire packets, windows instead of video memory. A programmer reads and writes files; a disk driver inside the OS translates that into head movements and sector addresses. Bottom-up, the OS is a resource manager. Many programs compete for the same CPU, memory and I/O devices, so the OS performs an orderly, controlled allocation of processors, memories and devices among them. Sharing (multiplexing) works in two ways. Time multiplexing lets programs take turns: the CPU executes one process for a few milliseconds, then another (printers work the same way — one job at a time). Space multiplexing splits the resource into parts used simultaneously: each program gets its own region of memory, each file its own disk blocks. Key Pitfall: the two views answer different questions. “Why can I ignore the disk geometry?” — extended machine. “Why does my program slow down when ten others run?” — resource manager. 1.2 Kernel Mode and User Mode Hardware would be defenceless if any program could execute any instruction: one buggy application could halt the machine or wipe a disk. Therefore most computers provide two execution modes. In kernel mode (supervisor mode) the OS runs with complete access to all hardware and may execute every instruction the machine supports. Everything else — browsers, mail readers, music players, the user interface itself — runs in user mode: only a subset of instructions is available, and anything affecting machine control or I/O is forbidden. A user program that needs a service (read a file, send a packet) cannot perform it directly; it issues a system call (TRAP), which traps into the kernel, runs the OS routine with full privileges, and returns the result. Conceptually the machine is layered: hardware at the bottom, the OS in kernel mode above it, and user-mode programs on top. Why it matters: isolation is what makes crashes survivable. A fault in a user-mode program kills only that program; the same fault in kernel mode halts the whole system (kernel panic / blue screen). Key Pitfall: device drivers must live in the OS, precisely so they can run in kernel mode and touch controller registers — that is also why a bad driver can crash the machine. 1.3 History of Operating Systems Each hardware generation forced a new kind of OS. Five dates and machines cover the whole story. 1st generation (1945–1955): vacuum tubes, plugboards. Colossus (Turing) and ENIAC (Mauchly): huge, slow, power-hungry, air-conditioned rooms, kilobytes of storage at best, programmed in machine language by rewiring. There was no OS at all — one program owned the whole machine. 2nd generation (1955–1965): transistors, batch systems. Transistors, core memory, magnetic tapes and disks; machines became smaller, cooler and cheaper. The first operating systems appeared to automate job sequencing on mainframes; programming moved to machine language and assembly. 3rd generation (1965–1980): integrated circuits. SSI/MSI chips, low power draw, high-level languages (Honeywell-6000, PDP, IBM-360/370). Three OS ideas born here still run the world: multiprogramming (several jobs in memory, CPU switches when one waits), spooling and timesharing. The second half (1971–1980) added microprocessors (LSI/VLSI): portable computers, RAID storage, data communication, fast large memories — and early uses in parallel processing, simulation, speech recognition and artificial intelligence. 4th generation (1980–1990): personal computers. LSI made a computer fit on a desk: the first microcomputer paired an Intel 8080 with an 8-inch floppy and ran CP/M (Control Program for Microcomputers), the first disk-based OS. IBM built the PC and contracted Bill Gates for its operating system. 5th generation (1990–present): mobile computers. From brick phones to touchscreen smartphones: the computer became a battery-powered, always-networked personal device. How to remember: hardware shrinks and multiplies, software centralises control — no OS, batch OS, multiprogramming OS, personal OS, mobile OS. 1.4 Computer Hardware Review An OS is tied to the hardware it runs on: it extends the instruction set and manages the resources. Five hardware areas matter. 1.4.1 Processors Every CPU repeats one cycle: fetch the next instruction into a buffer, decode the opcode and operands, calculate effective operand addresses, fetch operands from memory (register operands skip this), execute, write the result back. To hold the working state the CPU has registers: general registers for variables and temporaries, the program counter (address of the next instruction), the stack pointer (top of the in-memory stack), and the PSW (Program Status Word: comparison flags, CPU priority, kernel/user mode bit and other control bits). Raw speed comes from overlap. A three-stage pipeline (fetch → decode → execute units working on three instructions at once) and superscalar designs (parallel pipelines feeding parallel execute units through a holding buffer) do more per clock. Multithreading (hyper-threading) goes further: the CPU keeps the state of two threads and switches between them in nanoseconds, so when one thread stalls on a memory read the other runs — note this hides latency but is not true parallelism. True parallelism needs several cores: modern chips are multicore (a quad-core with a shared L2 cache versus separate L2 per core are the two textbook layouts), and a GPU is thousands of tiny cores for small parallel computations such as polygon rendering. Multicore hardware requires a multiprocessor OS. 1.4.2 Memory Memory is a hierarchy: each higher layer is faster, smaller and more expensive per bit. The lecture’s reference numbers are worth memorising: registers (~1 nsec, under 1 KB), cache (~2 nsec, ~4 MB), main memory (~10 nsec, 1–8 GB), magnetic disk (~10 msec, 1–4 TB). Main memory is divided into cache lines of typically 64 bytes; the hottest lines live in a cache inside the CPU. On a read, hardware checks the cache first: a hit costs about 2 clock cycles and no bus traffic, a miss goes to main memory. Machines often stack two or three cache levels, each slower and bigger. Cache design is four questions: when to insert, where to place, what to evict, and where the evicted item goes. Technologies differ in volatility. RAM serves whatever the cache cannot; ROM keeps factory-programmed contents without power (classically the bootstrap loader lives there); EEPROM and flash are also nonvolatile but erasable and rewritable — flash sits between RAM and disk in speed, backs phones and USB sticks, and wears out with writes. CMOS memory holds the clock, date and boot configuration such as which disk to boot from. Worked micro-example (average access time): with cache hit rate at cycles, RAM hit rate at cycles on a miss, disk cycles otherwise: The lesson: even a 2% trip to disk dominates everything — hierarchy performance is decided by miss rates, not by cache speed. 1.4.3 Disks A hard disk is a stack of platters; each surface is divided into concentric tracks, each track into sectors (an arc of a track is a segment). An actuator arm swings the read/write heads over the surfaces. Every access pays three costs: seek time (moving the head), rotation delay / latency (waiting for the sector to spin under the head) and transfer time (the actual bit flow, i.e. data rate). 1.4.4 I/O Devices Each device has two halves: a controller (electronics accepting OS commands) and the device itself (deliberately simple, standardised interface). The program that talks to the controller is the device driver; it must live in the OS to run in kernel mode. Controllers expose a few registers; the set of all of them is the I/O port space. Two addressing schemes exist: memory-mapped I/O (registers appear at ordinary memory addresses) and a separate port space with special IN/OUT instructions usable only in kernel mode. Getting data in and out has three generations. Busy waiting (polling): the driver starts the transfer and spins in a loop asking “done yet?” — simple, but the CPU is tied up. Interrupts: the driver starts the device, blocks the caller and does other work; on completion the controller raises an interrupt, the CPU vectors through the interrupt vector (a table mapping device numbers to handler addresses) into the handler, then returns to the user program. DMA (Direct Memory Access): a dedicated chip moves whole blocks between memory and controller with no CPU involvement; the CPU only programs the transfer and receives one interrupt at the end. Key Pitfall: interrupts do not make I/O faster — they free the CPU while I/O is in flight. DMA then removes even the per-byte CPU cost. 1.4.5 Buses Components meet at buses, and the OS must know every one for configuration. A shared bus (one set of wires, many devices) needs an arbiter deciding who transmits. A parallel bus spreads one word over many wires (classic PCI: 32 bits over 32 wires); a serial bus sends bits down one lane, scaling by adding lanes. Concrete buses: DDR3/DDR4 (CPU–RAM), PCIe (graphics), DMI (bridge-to-bridge hub link), SCSI/SATA (disks), USB (centralised: the root device polls every peripheral for traffic). Before Plug & Play, each card hard-coded its interrupt line and register addresses, so two cards could collide; Plug & Play enumerates devices and centrally assigns interrupts and addresses. 1.5 Booting the Computer Starting the machine is a relay race, in strict order. BIOS, a program on the motherboard with low-level I/O routines, runs first and performs POST (Power-On Self-Test): memory size, device presence, basic integrity. It then scans the buses to enumerate devices and picks the boot device from the list stored in CMOS memory. The first sector of that device — the boot sector — is loaded and executed; it reads the partition table at the sector’s end to find the active partition. A secondary boot loader from that partition loads the OS itself. The newborn OS queries the BIOS for the hardware inventory, checks it has a driver per device, loads the drivers into the kernel, initialises its tables, spawns background processes, and finally starts a login prompt or GUI. Why the order matters: each stage only knows how to load something slightly smarter than itself — ROM code cannot parse filesystems, so booting climbs BIOS → boot sector → loader → OS. 1.6 The OS Zoo Different machines need different operating systems. Mainframe OSs (OS/360, OS/390) live in data centres and are tuned for hundreds of concurrent I/O-heavy jobs. Server OSs (UNIX, Linux, Windows Server, FreeBSD, Solaris) serve many users over a network, sharing hardware and software. Multiprocessor OSs coordinate several CPUs — today every PC and notebook OS qualifies (Linux, Windows). Personal computer OSs need a single-user interactive system (Windows, macOS, Linux, FreeBSD). Handheld OSs target phones and tablets (Android, iOS). Embedded OSs hide inside devices that take no installed software — microwaves, MP3 players, TVs, cars (Embedded Linux, QNX, VxWorks). Sensor-node OSs (TinyOS) run on motes that are complete tiny computers — CPU, RAM, ROM plus environmental sensors, meshed over wireless to a base station. Real-time OSs keep deadlines: hard real-time guarantees the action happens in time, always; soft real-time tolerates an occasional miss without damage (QNX). Smart-card OSs are the smallest of all: a CPU on a credit card, often holding a JVM interpreter so downloaded applets run on the card. 2. Definitions Operating System: A system software that manages computer hardware resources and provides common services for computer programs. Resource Management: The primary function of an operating system to efficiently allocate hardware components like CPU, memory, and I/O devices among multiple programs. Abstraction: A mechanism provided by the operating system to hide complex bare-metal hardware details behind clean, simple interfaces. Multiprogramming: The allocation and execution of multiple programs on a single computer system simultaneously. Time-sharing: A logical extension of multiprogramming where computing resources are shared among several users concurrently through rapid context switching. Kernel Mode: A privileged execution mode in which code has complete and unrestricted access to all underlying hardware and memory addresses. User Mode: A restricted execution mode where applications cannot directly access hardware or reference memory, requiring system APIs to perform privileged operations. Hyperthreading: A technology that allows a single physical CPU core to execute multiple threads concurrently by providing duplicate logical processors. Virtual Memory: A memory management capability that uses disk storage to extend apparent physical RAM capacity. 3. Practice 3.1. OS Functions (Tutorial 1, Problem 1.1) What are the two main functions of an operating system? Click to see the solution The two main functions are: 1. Resource management: Efficiently allocating CPU, memory, storage, and I/O devices among competing processes and users. 2. Providing fine abstractions from the bare metal: Presenting clean, uniform, and high-level virtual interfaces (such as files, processes, and sockets) to hide the complex and heterogeneous underlying hardware details. Answer: Resource management and hardware abstraction. 3.2. Time-Sharing vs Multiprogramming (Tutorial 1, Problem 1.3) What is the difference between time-sharing and multiprogramming systems? Click to see the solution Multiprogramming is the basic allocation and concurrent retention of multiple programs in main memory simultaneously, allowing the CPU to switch to another program when one is waiting for I/O, thereby maximizing CPU utilization. Time-sharing (or multitasking) is a logical extension of multiprogramming where CPU resources are rapidly shared among several interactive users or processes using timer interrupts, giving each user the illusion of dedicated access to the machine. Relationship: All time-sharing systems are multiprogramming systems, but not all multiprogramming systems are time-sharing systems (some early multiprogramming systems ran batch jobs without interactive user turnaround). Answer: Time-sharing extends multiprogramming with rapid CPU sharing; every time-sharing system is multiprogramming, not vice versa. 3.3. Kernel Mode and User Mode (Tutorial 1, Problem 1.10) What is the difference between kernel mode and user mode, and how does this dual-mode design aid operating system construction? Click to see the solution Kernel Mode: Executing code has complete, unrestricted access to the underlying hardware. It can execute any privileged CPU instruction and reference any physical or virtual memory address. Crashes in kernel mode are catastrophic and halt the entire operating system (kernel panic / BSOD). User Mode: Executing code operates under hardware-enforced restrictions. It cannot directly access hardware devices or reference arbitrary memory locations. Applications must invoke system calls (APIs) to request kernel services on their behalf. Design Aid: This isolation protects system stability and security. Because user-mode applications cannot directly corrupt critical hardware state or other users’ memory spaces, bugs and crashes in user mode are completely isolated and fully recoverable. Answer: Kernel mode runs unrestricted, user mode is restricted to syscalls — faults stay isolated. 3.4. title: W1. Foundations of Probability
text: 1. Theory 1.1 Random Experiments, Outcomes, and Sample Spaces A random experiment is any repeatable physical observation, measurement, or procedure whose outcome cannot be predicted with absolute certainty in advance, but whose set of all conceivable results can be fully cataloged before execution. An individual, indivisible result of a single realization of a random experiment is called an elementary outcome (or sample point), denoted by . The collection of all possible elementary outcomes forms the universal set of the experiment, termed the sample space, denoted by (or ). Every performance of the experiment terminates in precisely one outcome . The outcomes comprising must be: Mutually exclusive: No two distinct outcomes ( ) can occur simultaneously on a single trial. Collectively exhaustive: At least one outcome must occur whenever the experiment is performed. 1.1.1 Why Formalizing the Sample Space Matters In probability theory, probabilities cannot be assigned in an abstract void; they are defined strictly as set functions over subsets of a predetermined reference universe. Choosing and precisely specifying defines the universe of discourse. An ambiguous, incomplete, or ill-defined sample space undermines the subsequent assignment of probabilities, leading directly to logical paradoxes and invalid normalizations. 1.1.2 Classification of Sample Spaces by Cardinality The mathematical structure of a probability model depends fundamentally on the cardinality of the sample space: Finite Sample Spaces ( ): The set contains a finite number of discrete elements. Tossing a single coin: , with . Rolling a standard six-sided die: , with . Tossing a coin three consecutive times: Countably Infinite Sample Spaces ( ): The outcomes can be arranged in an infinite sequence and placed in a one-to-one correspondence with the non-negative integers . Network traffic monitoring: Counting the total number of email packets arriving at a mail server within a fixed one-hour window: Repeated trials until success: Tossing a coin repeatedly until the first Head appears, recording the total number of tosses required: . Uncountably Infinite (Continuous) Sample Spaces ( ): The outcomes form a continuum and cannot be listed or indexed by the integers; they represent intervals or regions in Euclidean space . Component reliability: The operational lifespan of an electronic component until failure: Analog electrical measurements: The instantaneous voltage across a noisy resistor: . Thermodynamic tracking: A continuous temperature measurement: (or on the Kelvin scale). Particle physics: The exact spatial coordinates of a subatomic particle inside a reaction chamber: . Signal sampling: The exact arrival time (in milliseconds) of an atmospheric static electrical pulse captured by a radio receiver. 1.1.3 The Granularity Principle A physical experiment does not possess a uniquely mandated mathematical sample space. The choice of is an abstraction dictated entirely by the observer’s engineering or experimental objectives. The same physical trial can be described by sample spaces of differing granularity: Consider rolling a standard six-sided die: If the objective is to observe the exact face that lands upward: If the objective is only to record the parity of the score: Sample space has finer granularity than . It provides strictly more information: knowledge of an outcome in uniquely determines the corresponding outcome in (e.g., observing immediately implies the outcome is ). Conversely, observing does not reveal whether the true face in was or . The macro-outcomes of correspond to a non-overlapping partition of the micro-outcomes of : 1.1.4 Worked Mini-Illustration: Quality Testing of Microchips An automated test station evaluates two microchips off an assembly line sequentially. Each chip is classified either as passing ( ) or defective ( ). Detailed Sample Space (Order-Preserving): If the technician tracks the individual identity and order of the chips: Coarse Sample Space (Defect Count): If the quality engineer only logs the total number of defective units found in the batch of two: The mapping between the granular spaces maps , , and . Both formulations are mathematically valid descriptions of the experiment, but is required if one needs to determine whether the first chip specifically was defective. 1.1.5 Common Pitfalls Confusing Outcomes with Events: An outcome is an indivisible element of the set ( ). An event is a subset of ( ). While a singleton set contains only one outcome, it is formally an event, not an outcome: . Violating Mutual Exclusivity: Constructing candidate sample spaces whose elements overlap. For instance, proposing for a single die roll fails because the roll is simultaneously even and prime, violating the requirement that exactly one element of occurs per trial. Assuming Uniform Likelihood on Coarse Spaces: Coarse spaces constructed by aggregating granular outcomes do not inherit uniform probabilities. In the microchip illustration, even if each chip in has an equal chance of passing or failing (making all 4 sequence outcomes equally likely with probability ), the elements in are not equally likely: outcome corresponds to and thus has twice the probability of outcome ( ) or outcome ( ). 1.2 Events, Set Operations, and Algebraic Identities An event is a subset of the sample space (written ). We say that the event occurs in a trial of a random experiment if the realized outcome is an element of , that is, . The collection of all observable events is denoted by . Events are classified according to their structure and cardinality: An elementary event (or simple event) consists of a single individual outcome: a singleton set . A compound event contains two or more distinct outcomes, formed by grouping elementary outcomes together (for example, rolling an even number on a six-sided die: ). The certain event is the entire sample space itself. Because every valid trial produces some outcome , the certain event occurs inevitably in every execution of the experiment. The impossible event (or null event) is the empty set (also denoted ). It contains no sample points; hence, it can never occur. 1.2.1 Why Event Formalism Matters Translating experimental hypotheses into set-theoretic structures replaces informal verbal statements with unambiguous mathematical objects. When events are formalized as subsets of , probabilistic questions about combinations of occurrences (“both happen”, “at least one happens”, “neither happens”) translate directly into rigorous operations of Boolean algebra. 1.2.2 Event Operations and Set Relations Let and be two events associated with the same sample space . New events are generated through standard set operations: Complement: The complement of an event with respect to , denoted by (or ), is the set of all outcomes in that do not belong to : represents the event that does not occur. Intersection: The intersection of two events and , denoted , is the event containing all outcomes that belong simultaneously to both and : represents the joint occurrence of both and . Union: The union of two events and , denoted , is the event containing all outcomes that belong to , to , or to both: represents the occurrence of at least one of the two events. Set Difference: The difference of event and event , denoted , is the set of outcomes belonging to but not to : represents the event that occurs while fails to occur. Mutual Exclusivity: Two events and are mutually exclusive (or disjoint) if they share no outcomes: Mutually exclusive events cannot occur simultaneously in a single trial. 1.2.3 Fundamental Algebraic Identities For any event , the following identities hold algebraically: (annihilation under intersection) (identity under union) (law of non-contradiction) (law of excluded middle) and (involution) , where (disjoint decomposition) 1.2.4 De Morgan’s Laws and Logical Proof De Morgan’s laws state that the complement of an intersection is the union of the complements, and the complement of a union is the intersection of the complements: For an arbitrary index set (including finite and countably infinite collections): Element-Wise Logical Proof of : To establish equality of the two sets, we verify that an arbitrary outcome belongs to the left-hand side if and only if it belongs to the right-hand side using two-way logical equivalences ( ): Because the chain of equivalences holds bidirectionally, . Element-Wise Logical Proof of : Thus, . In event terminology: “neither nor occurs” is identical to “at least one of or fails to occur” being false. 1.2.5 Worked Illustration: Server Cluster Reliability Consider a computing cluster of three servers. Let denote the event “server is operational”, for . We express operational states as set operations: All three servers are operational: At least one server is down: Using the complement of and De Morgan’s law: Exactly one server is operational: Decomposed as three mutually exclusive events corresponding to which specific server is up while the other two are down: At least two servers are operational: Formed by the union of pairs: The case where all three are operational is automatically subsumed, since . 1.2.6 Common Pitfalls Mutually Exclusive vs. Independent: Mutual exclusivity is a purely set-theoretic property ( : the sets do not overlap). Independence is a probabilistic property ( ). Two non-empty events with non-zero probability can never be both mutually exclusive and independent. The Empty Set vs. : The empty set contains no elements whatsoever ( ). In contrast, is a valid non-empty elementary event containing the numerical outcome (for instance, receiving zero errors on an interface). Asymmetry of Set Difference: Unlike union and intersection, set difference is non-commutative: in general. represents “ occurs and does not”, whereas represents “ occurs and does not”. 1.3 Empirical and Classical Models of Probability The bridge between physical observation and abstract mathematical modeling is established through two foundational frameworks: the empirical model based on observed frequencies and the classical model based on physical symmetry. 1.3.1 Empirical Probability and the Frequency Stabilization Principle The empirical probability (or relative frequency probability) of an event approximates its likelihood of occurrence via empirical observation. Suppose an experiment is repeated independently times under identical conditions. If event occurs in exactly of these trials, the relative frequency is defined as: The empirical probability assigns: The operational validity of this definition rests on the empirical observation known as the frequency stabilization principle: as the number of independent trials grows arbitrarily large ( ), the relative frequency ceases to fluctuate erratically and stabilizes around a distinct, constant numerical value : The systematic nature of frequency stabilization is demonstrated empirically by tracking the number of heads obtained across repeated sequences of coin tosses of length , , and : Series ( ) ( ) ( ) ( ) 1 41 4985 499558 2 48 5004 499952 3 44 5085 500114 4 52 4946 500064 5 58 4978 500183 6 52 4985 499533 7 45 5012 500065 8 50 4931 500317 9 52 5016 500449 10 45 4973 500704 Typical Error ( ) At , relative frequencies range from to , producing an absolute deviation of order from the theoretical value . When scaled to , the ratio contracts to the interval (error ). At , the values concentrate tightly within , establishing an error bound bounded by . 1.3.2 The Classical (Laplace) Probability Model While the empirical model operates a posteriori (after collecting data), the classical definition of probability operates a priori by deducing probabilities from the geometric or physical symmetries of the experiment. Let be a finite sample space containing mutually exclusive elementary outcomes: . If all elementary outcomes are equally likely (equiprobable) due to physical symmetry, then each outcome must carry identical probability mass: For any compound event consisting of favorable outcomes, the classical probability of is the ratio of the cardinality of to the cardinality of : 1.3.3 Worked Mini-Illustration Consider a batch containing components, of which are defective and are functional. An inspector samples items uniformly at random without replacement. Total Sample Space Size: Any selection of items from is equally likely. Thus: Event (Zero Defective Items Selected): All chosen components must come from the functional components: Event (Exactly One Defective Item Selected): Choose of the defectives and of the functional components: 1.3.4 Limitations and Common Pitfalls Both models possess structural limitations that prevent them from serving as universal mathematical foundations: Limitations of the Empirical Model: It requires experiments that are infinitely and independently repeatable under invariant physical conditions. Phenomena that are singular, unique (e.g., forecasting the probability of an unprecedented geopolitical or macroeconomic event), or non-stationary cannot be evaluated empirically. Furthermore, for any finite , yields only an empirical estimate, never the exact theoretical probability. Limitations of the Classical Model: It strictly requires a finite sample space and hinges upon the assumption of equiprobability. Assuming equal likelihood in systems lacking physical symmetry leads to fallacious conclusions. Common Pitfall — Circular Reasoning: Defining classical probability as the ratio of favorable to total outcomes when all outcomes are equally likely is inherently circular: “equally likely” means having “equal probability,” using the concept of probability to define probability itself. This circularity necessitated Kolmogorov’s axiomatic formulation. 1.4 Discrete Probability Spaces with Non-Uniform Weights The classical probability model assumes that all elementary outcomes are equally likely, assigning an identical mass to each sample point. However, real-world physical systems frequently exhibit structural imbalances, manufacturing asymmetries, or heterogeneous frequencies. To accommodate these scenarios, probability theory generalizes discrete models by assigning an individual non-negative parameter—termed an outcome weight or elementary probability—to each individual point in the sample space. Let be a finite or countably infinite sample space. An elementary probability assignment (or weight function) is a mapping associating each elementary outcome with a real weight such that: Non-negativity: Every outcome weight is non-negative: Total Probability Weight Condition (Normalization): The aggregate weight of all mutually exclusive elementary outcomes in the universe equals unity: For any arbitrary compound event , the probability of an event under this weighted measure is defined by the discrete aggregation of the weights of all sample points comprising : By construction, this formulation naturally guarantees , , and , aligning directly with finite and countable additivity over disjoint elementary singletons. 1.4.1 Biased System Modeling: The Loaded Die When constructing a weighted probability model, relative qualitative descriptions (such as “twice as likely”) are translated into an algebraic system constrained by the normalization condition . Consider a standard six-sided die that has been loaded such that each even face is twice as likely to appear as each odd face. The sample space of elementary outcomes is: Let denote the probability weight assigned to each individual odd outcome: Because each even outcome is twice as likely as an odd outcome, the weight assigned to each even outcome is: Applying the total probability weight condition across the entire sample space: Substituting the parameter expressions: Thus, the discrete probability mass function over the singletons is: 1.4.2 Compound Event Probabilities via Weighted Summation Once the individual outcome weights are established, probabilities of compound events are obtained by identifying the constituent elements of each event set and summing their respective weights. Using the loaded die model above, consider the following events: Event (“rolling a number strictly less than 4”): The subset is . Its probability is: Event (“rolling an even number”) and Event (“rolling a number divisible by 3”): Here, and . The joint event (intersection) represents obtaining an even number divisible by 3: The union represents obtaining a number that is even, divisible by 3, or both: Summing the constituent weights directly yields: Alternatively, applying the general addition rule verifies consistency: 1.4.3 Common Pitfalls Falling back to cardinal counting: A frequent mistake is applying the classical ratio formula to biased spaces. In the loaded die example, and , which would erroneously suggest . The correct probability is , because outcomes carry unequal measures of likelihood. Cardinal counting is valid if and only if for every outcome . Normalizing against relative ratios rather than unity: When given relative ratios (e.g., ), students sometimes omit the normalization equation , setting and . Probabilities must strictly belong to the interval . The relative multipliers must always be scaled by dividing by the sum of all weights across . 1.5 Geometric Probability on Continuous Domains When a random experiment generates outcomes from an uncountably infinite set, the classical discrete ratio becomes mathematically undefined because , while individual singleton outcomes have probability zero. Geometric probability resolves this limitation by extending the principle of equally likely outcomes to continuous domains through geometric measure.
